speechtext:
1.	How many employees have been laid off by the Canadian National Railways since September 1, 1953?
2.	How many of such employees were, at the time of their being laid off, between the ages of 60 and 65?
3.	How many of such employees between the ages of 60 and 65 are in receipt of any pension from the Canadian National Railways, and what is the average amount of such pension?
4.	How many of such employees between the ages of 60 and 65 have been laid off without any pension?
5.	What steps are being taken by the Canadian National Railways to provide a pension for such employees?

subtopic: CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS LAY-OFFS
speechtext:
Perhaps I might be allowed to deal with this question orally, Mr. Speaker.
The management of the Canadian National Railways informs me that to answer an inquiry of the general character of part 1 of the question would necessitate the examination of innumerable local records in 42 divisions of the railway all across Canada, and would require the services of a considerable staff for many weeks.
In this connection, it is pointed out to me that the Canadian National regularly compiles a substantial volume of statistical data of all kinds relating to the business of the company, and these statistics are regularly published by the dominion bureau of statistics in a monthly report entitled "railway operating statistics".
Referring specifically to parts 2, 3, 4 and 5 of the question, the management advise that lay-olfs, when made, are strictly in accordance with the seniority principles prescribed in the agreements with employees' organizations, and that it would be most unusual for an employee aged 60 or over to have his employment status indefinitely, but not permanently, severed. Eligibility for pension under the Canadian National Railways pension rules depends on the attainment of a certain age and the accumulation of a certain number of years of service.

While the Family Allowances Act and regulations disqualify from receipt of the allowance any child of school age who improperly absents himself from school, the policy of the Department of National Health and Welfare is to accept the interpretation of the provincial school inspection authorities on this point. What is the Department of National Health and Welfare doing to ensure that supplies of Salk polio vaccine are made available to the provinces for their use this year?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
In anticipation of the
ultimate availability of an effective vaccine for poliomyelitis, planning and expansion of activities in the Department of National Health and Welfare have been geared to cope
Manitoba
Sask	
Alberta . . B.C	

Questions
with the demands expected to result from a development of this nature in the poliomyelitis field. At this time it is not possible to offer any prediction on the outcome of the vaccine trials in the United States. Nevertheless, in co-operation with the provinces the federal government has taken steps to ensure the availability of supplies of a vaccine for further trials this year.
Important steps have been taken in two general areas, research and the production of the vaccine.
Under the national health grants program, a special research effort is being supported at Connaught medical research laboratories in Toronto and the Institute of Microbiology and Hygiene in Montreal. At the former, investigation of the antigenic types of poliomyelitis present in Canada, studies of the poliomyelitis virus, its cultivation in tissue culture and the development of a vaccine have been assisted. At the Montreal institution, research on neurotropic virus, epidemiology of the disease and studies of poliomyelitis virus in tissue culture have also been supported with special grants. Altogether in these and other institutions in the present fiscal year over $83,000 has been earmarked for research in the field of poliomyelitis and related problems out of the public health research grant. During the previous year allocations for research in this area approximated $60,000. Neither of these amounts takes into consideration the extensive support provided under the national health grants program for blood fractionation and the production of gamma globulin.
In the laboratory of hygiene of the Department of National Health and Welfare, a special section dealing with virus research has been actively engaged in studies on the poliomyelitis virus and methods of testing a vaccine. There is another section in the laboratory which deals with tissue culture which is important in the propagation of poliomyelitis virus for the development of a vaccine.
Funds under the national health grants program are being provided for the processing of sufficient vaccine for the Canadian trials this year. The Connaught medical research laboratories have been engaged in preparing a large part of the culture fluids for poliomyelitis virus which were used by pharmaceutical manufacturers in the United States last year. It was possible therefore for them to undertake the preparation of the vaccine on behalf of the federal and provincial departments of health. For this purpose assistance is being provided under the general public health grant with the total expenditure

being shared by federal and provincial governments. This broad project involves the commitment of up to $375,000 national health grant funds with an equal amount from provincial sources. It has been planned that each provincial department of health will receive a proportionate share of the vaccine and will arrange for the trial of this material.
The biologies control and virus sections of the laboratory of hygiene have given special attention to poliomyelitis vaccine during the past three or four months. In close co-operation with the Connaught medical research laboratories, the vaccine is being retested for safety before it will be released to provincial authorities. This work is carried on under the authority of the Food and Drugs Act and is designed to give added protection as regards safety.

subtopic: ADVISABILITY OF BALLOT WITH RESPECT TO PAYMENT OF MEMBERSHIP DUES
ADVISABILITY OF BALLOT WITH RESPECT TO PAYMENT OF MEMBERSHIP DUES
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should consider the advisability of empowering the Canadian wheat board to conduct a ballot, by mail, of the grain producers holding permit books to ascertain the wishes of such producers as to the wheat board complying with orders signed by such producers directing the wheat board to pay membership dues to farm organizations from money due such producers from the sale of their grain by the wheat board.
He said: May I first of all express my thanks and appreciation to you, Mr. Speaker, for having on my behalf asked for unanimous consent to have this motion retain its place on the order paper during my unavoidable absence. I also thank hon. members for having granted such a request.
The purpose of this resolution is to consider the advisability of the government empowering the Canadian wheat board to conduct a ballot by mail of grain producers of the three prairie provinces, who hold permit books, for the purpose of ascertaining whether or not it is the desire or the wish of farmers to have farm organizations' dues deducted by the Canadian wheat board from moneys owing to them from the sale of their grain. Hon. members know, of course, that in the three prairie provinces the farmer is required by law to sell his grain through the Canadian wheat board. The farmer receives an initial payment, followed by subsequent interim and final payments. The producers hold permit books, and of course the balloting which is referred to in this resolution would be confined to the three prairie provinces. Therefore, if the producers who hold permit books, through such a ballot, were to express a desire to have farm organizations' dues so deducted, and if the wheat board were to agree to this arrangement, then such moneys owing to

permit holders would be deducted by the wheat board to pay farm organization dues.
I know that many hon. members hold very strong views with regard to the check-off system. Let me point out that in supporting this resolution hon. members are not dedicated either directly, or even by implication, to the support of the check-off system. What they would be doing is to leave it to the farmer to decide for himself whether or not he is in favour of voluntary requisition of farm organization dues. Let me read the resolution as it appears on the order paper:
That, in the opinion ol this house, the government should consider the advisability of empowering the Canadian wheat board to conduct a ballot, by mail, of the grain producers holding permit books to ascertain the wishes of such producers as to the wheat board complying with orders signed by such producers directing the wheat board to pay membership dues to farm organizations from money due such producers from the sale of their grain by the wheat board.
It can be readily seen, therefore, that it will be up to the farmer alone to decide whether or not he is in favour of the voluntary requisition. Assume that this resolution was to pass the house, and assume further that the government considered the matter carefully and did in fact empower the Canadian wheat board to conduct such a ballot. Then, as I say, it is up to the farmer to express his views or desires through such a ballot as to whether or not he would like to have this kind of plan in operation.
The procedure is quite simple. There is nothing unusual about it. It is just one method in our democratic system of finding out what the views of the farmers are in this regard. If the producers through such balloting showed their opposition to this plan, then of course the matter would end right there. On the other hand, if the results of such balloting indicated to the satisfaction of the wheat board that a substantial majority of the producers were in favour of having their farm organization dues so deducted by the wheat board and in the manner suggested by this resolution, then what would the position be? Let me point out that in this resolution there is nothing which suggests compulsion either to belong to any farm organization or to compel the farmer to have his farm dues deducted by the wheat board. And of course there certainly should be some provision for the revocation by the farmer at any time he so desired of an order that he may have directed to the wheat board. In this case it would apply only to those farmers who voluntarily, of their own free will, signed an order to the wheat board for the deduction of such dues.

One of the objections that might be raised to this plan by some hon. members would be the argument that there may be a considerable number of farmers who would not want the wheat board to undertake such a task. It might be argued that every farmer in the country would be forced to pay the cost of deduction, bookkeeping and transmission of funds involved in this plan. In other words, those farmers who are not prepared to become members of a farm organization, or will not wish to have the deduction made at the source, might say that they should not be penalized by being forced to help pay the cost of a scheme when they get no benefit from it. Let me point out that all such expenses or costs should be borne by those who wish to have their farm membership dues so deducted, should this plan eventually come into operation. I might also point out that the interprovincial farm union council have stated that they are prepared and are willing to pay for the cost of administration and the collection of those dues. Furthermore, the taxpayer of Canada will not be required in any way at all to contribute to the cost of placing this plan in operation.
Some question has been raised with regard to the initial cost of the conducting of this ballot. There again I think the Canadian wheat board and the interprovincial farm union council should get together and find out a method of financing this type of ballot.
It will be noted that the resolution calls for the conducting of the ballot by mail. Although it will no doubt involve a considerable amount of work and some expense, it will be nothing of the type that one would envisage in the conducting of an election.
I am proposing this resolution, Mr. Speaker, at the request of the interprovincial farm union council, which includes in it the farm union of Alberta, the Saskatchewan farmers union and the Manitoba farmers union. I have in mind also another important farm organization, namely, the Canadian Federation of Agriculture. I am not certain whether or not they have direct membership dues payable, but I do feel that the Canadian Federation of Agriculture could also benefit from this scheme or plan, should it be found necessary for them to change their constitution.
In proposing this resolution, Mr. Speaker, I am motivated by the desire to see strong and healthy farm organizations. I think a good, strong farm organization is invaluable in making suggestions and giving advice, whether it be to provincial or to federal governments. I think it is something that is necessary in our Canadian economy. If you were to consider the past history of farm 50433-85
Canadian Wheat Board organizations in Canada you would find that it has been one of ups and downs, due mainly to financial instability.
A very substantial percentage of their budget each year is spent in collecting membership fees. Should a good majority of the farmers agree to this plan, then all this unnecessary expense, as well as the time consumed in the collection of farm union dues, would be eliminated and would leave the farm organization leaders with a greater share of their budget and more time for the expansion of their programs.
Agriculture is our basic industry, especially so in the three prairie provinces. In a healthy democracy such as ours the rise of influence and power of farm organizations must be met by a corresponding rise in the measure of responsibility of their leaders. The farm organizations in the three prairie provinces have in recent years risen to considerable influence and power, with the result that this is accompanied by corresponding rise in the measure of responsibility on the part of such organizations.
I am convinced that our responsible farm organizations in Canada are past the point now where they consider a program of protest alone as being fitting or proper. It does not mean that at times protest is likely to be undesirable. What I wish to bring out is that responsible leaders of farm organizations realize this, as is indicated by Dr. Hannam in his message to the nineteenth annual convention of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture held recently in Edmonton. In referring to responsible farm organizations, he said that such an organization:
-cannot merely voice a demand, toss all Its serious problems on the doorstep of the government and then pack up and go home. On the contrary- it is expected to tell the federal ministers how what they demand might be accomplished. In other words constructive leadership to its industry, and a constructive approach to national programs, should go hand in hand with the maturity and the strength achieved by the Canadian Federation of Agriculture.
I am sure that all of us in this house will agree with those words of Dr. Hannam. That is what every sound-thinking Canadian would expect from leaders of large farm organizations in this country.
In urging hon. members to support this resolution let me point out, first, that they are in no way dedicating themselves to the support of the check-off system, not even by implication. They are leaving the matter for the farmer to decide in a democratic way, and to decide for himself as to whether or not he is in favour of the voluntary requisition of farm organization dues.
Should a substantial majority of farmers favour this plan, there is no compulsion,

Canadian Wheat Board either to belong to any farm organization or to have dues collected. Finally, I feel that in voting for this resolution hon. members would be expressing their desire to assist in the building up of farm organizations in this country, which I believe are necessary and desirable in our Canadian economy.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, from time to time the question of the check-off has been aired in this house with reference to industrial labour organizations. I believe that this is the first time we have had an opportunity of discussing the voluntary revocable check-off in connection with farm organizations. I should like to express appreciation to the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Decore) for providing an opportunity for such discussion through his resolution.
It is a matter of only a week or so ago that the house voted on this issue as it applied to industrial organizations. As the topic was very thoroughly aired at that time, at least the mechanics of the subject, it will not be necessary now to go into all the details.
The idea of the check-off is gradually receiving acceptance across Canada among various groups. Many of the industrial organizations have it, teachers' organizations have it, and some civil servants-the postmasters, for example-have the check-off.
I am particularly interested in this resolution because it does not ask hon. members of the house to declare themselves either for or against the principle of the check-off. As the hon. member for Vegreville indicated in his opening remarks, it is merely recommending that the farmers themselves be given an opportunity to express their desires in this regard. I believe that this places the responsibility of decision right where it should rest, at the farm level itself.
It is quite significant that farm organizations should be thinking at this time in terms of the check-off. I agree with the hon. member for Vegreville that it is a healthy sign when we find farmers becoming concerned and preoccupied with problems relating to organization. It has always been most difficult to organize farmers because of the peculiar geographical conditions under which they live. They have had to work against the problem of isolation. Whenever unions have been organized or farm groups have been organized on a union basis it has been necessary for them to have an indirect type of membership because of the difficulty of collecting annual dues. Almost 50 per cent of the amount collected annually is eaten up in the expense of collecting by this method.
IMr. Decore.]

When we have an indication from the farmers themselves that they desire a more solid financial base for their organizations, that should be recognized. If the principle of this resolution is carried out it would give the farmers an opportunity of expressing their wishes on the subject.
One of the reasons why farmers are becoming more interested in organization today is the difficult conditions prevailing in the agricultural industry. Prices are going down and costs are rising. As a result of this price squeeze the farmers are becoming more concerned about the necessity of getting together as organized groups so that they may speak with a united voice on agricultural matters.
In the past, because of the difficulty of organizing farm producers, there has been a tendency in Canada for farm protest to express itself in the form of political outburst, upsurges of political movements and political parties. This was the case back in the twenties with the rise of the progressive movement in Canada; it was largely a farm political party. The experience of that party has demonstrated that it is not necessarily in the best interest of Canada as a whole for any one group to organize itself as a direct political expression. I therefore think it is imperative, if the farmers are to have the necessary united voice to speak on problems relating to their activities, that they have some method whereby they can form a solid farm organization.
Of course there are precautions that are necessary in carrying out a program of this kind. The hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Decore) has referred to some of them. When a subject of this nature is discussed I believe there will be the tendency to criticize it from this point of view: the resolution suggests using the wheat board organization as the means for deducting farm union dues. I would imagine that in this discussion criticism will be raised to the effect that once you open the door to deduction from wheat board funds for one particular purpose, you must face the possibility of having wide open blanket assignments. For example, a suggestion might be put forward that a creditor, wishing to collect a debt that he holds against a farmer, could approach the wheat board and ask for a similar assignment. If that criticism should arise, I think it is beside the point; because it should be quite easy to define the terms of any check-off arrangement so that it would be quite specific as to the purpose of the deduction. There is also, of course, the other matter that should be emphasized-and I believe the resolution mentions this fact-namely that the proposed

check-off scheme on which the farmers would be voting under this plebiscite arrangement would be a voluntary scheme; that is, they would have a choice in the matter. It should also be revocable. These provisions would put them in a position almost similar to that with respect to hail insurance where the farmer can take it out if he so wishes and he can withdraw from any scheme of this kind if he so desires after having once participated in it.
Generally, Mr. Speaker, with these reservations and brief statement of some precautions, I support the resolution that is before the house.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we in this group intend to support the resolution. The hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Decore) has pointed out that in supporting the resolution members are not committed to support of the voluntary requisition or check-off of farm union dues from payments owed the farmers by the wheat board. On the other hand, we have supported the principle of the voluntary check-off so far as labour is concerned, and we will certainly support it so far as the farmers are concerned.
The resolution is of a very general character. If it passes it does not actually commit the wheat board to take any action even though the government brings in a bill to empower the wheat board to take a ballot, because if you empower a body to do a certain thing you do not necessarily force it to do it. However, I presume if such a bill were introduced the wheat board would no doubt take action. The hon. member for Vegreville stated that if the majority of farmers supported the idea of such requisitions being honoured the wheat board could then go ahead, but even if only a minority of the farmers support the idea I can see no reason why the wheat board would not be prepared to accept requisitions from such minority instead of waiting for a majority to sign. The majority would not be penalized in any way by the wheat board honouring the requisitions of the minority.
A ballot could be conducted at very little expense. No doubt forms could be printed which could be sent to the farmers at the time their cheques are mailed to them, so there would be no extra expense involved. The interprovincial farm union has stated that if there is any objection to the expense entailed they would be quite prepared to pay the cost of executing the requisitions. The principle of the voluntary check-off has been very widely recognized throughout the country both in labour and in other organizations. I would say that there is actually far greater need of such action with respect to farm organizations than there is with respect to labour organizations for the simple reason that the farmers are so widely scattered throughout the country that it is very difficult indeed to get in touch with them in order to get them to pay their dues. In the past it has been necessary to do that each year.

I know that tor many years that job used to fall upon me in our locality. I invariably seemed to be one of those chosen to go around and collect farm union dues, and it meant a great deal of driving. Half the time it would happen that the farmer was away from home or somewhere out in the fields where he was very hard to find. It took a lot of time, and the whole process had to be repeated the following year. If the procedure outlined in the resolution is adopted and the requisitions are honoured by the wheat board, then they would remain in force indefinitely until such time as they were revoked by the farmers. I think the procedure would be a very simple and inexpensive one and would certainly be of great value to the farm organizations.
As some other members have pointed out, it is essential that we do all we can to help the farm organizations to build up their strength. Farmers today are beginning to face quite a critical situation. You have a situation where farm organizations, in one way, have to compete with labour organizations. Labour organizations are strongly organized, but farm organizations are weakly organized. I should like to see the farm organizations build up their strength so that they would be as strong as the labour organizations. When farm organization leaders came to Ottawa they could then speak for a very large percentage of the farmers of the country. I am satisfied that the government would pay far more attention to the representatives of farm organizations if they could say that they represented 60 per cent, 70 per cent or more of the farmers of the country. They would be speaking with a strong voice and, as I say, the government would be more liable to pay attention to their requests. While the resolution does not commit a person to the support of the voluntary requisition, I can say without hesitation that so far as this group is concerned we support a system of voluntary requisition.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it will be noted by the house that the whole purpose of the resolution is to give farmers the right to indicate whether they want the wheat board to honour orders to pay dues to farm organizations. As the wheat board is now constituted, no assignment of any money coming to a farmer and no order on money in the hands of the wheat board that is coming to any farmer is honoured, the idea being that the money in the hands of the wheat board should be free from any possibility of being seized by creditors or in any way attached or assigned. In other words, the purpose is so that the farmers can be
Canadian Wheat Board sure of getting their money. That has been the established basis upon which the wheat board has been operating.
When the farm union people suggested to me that an exception should be made in regard to farm union dues, I pointed out to them that that would be a change from the established basis of operation. I expressed some doubt as to whether farmers in general would want to change that situation in any way. If this were done in connection with farm union dues, then the money might no longer be regarded as the farmer's and might be subject to assignment or attachment. I said that so far as I could find out I thought the majority of the farmers in the area where I lived would be against making that change in the wheat board act.
The response of the farm union representative to me was that he was satisfied the farmers would support that change. As he pointed out, other parts of our community are strongly organized. The professional field is strongly organized and certain branches of the labour fields are also strongly organized. The argument was that we seem to be coming into a period where the farmer is facing a declining income but his costs are rising or, in some respects, remaining stable. It was felt that if the farmer, in his turn, did not organize he was not going to get a fair deal under our economic system.
The representative of the farm union said, if the farmers want this, and it is their money, why should they not have the right to dispose of it as they see fit, especially if it is on a voluntary basis. He said, if there is any difference of opinion as to whether or not farmers want this privilege, why not make some provision for a vote to be held to decide the matter? My response to that was, in effect, that I could easily understand that the government, being responsible for the operations of the wheat board and answerable to the farmers and to the people generally if the wheat board were not successful, could not abdicate its right to make decisions as to what should be done by the wheat board concerning matters vital to its success. If the wheat board did not operate successfully then, of course, the government would be held responsible. Since the government must answer to the farmers for the manner in which the wheat board operates, they could not make that right subject to the outcome of any plebiscite.
If the matter did not affect the successful functioning of the wheat board as a marketing agency, and if it merely concerned the right of the farmer to dispose of any money to his credit in the hands of the wheat board, then whether it was done or not done

Canadian Wheat Board did not seem to me to have any possible effect on the successful functioning of the wheat board as a marketing agency. Since the question did not go to the root of whether or not the wheat board could function successfully, it seemed to me that the democratic way of dealing with the matter would be to permit the farmers themselves to decide. Of course, the purpose of the motion made by the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Decore) is just that. By voting for this resolution no one says he is favourable to the check-off or whatever you might call it, and no one says he is against it. All he is saying is that the wheat board should be empowered to hold a vote of the permit holders to ascertain whether or not they would like the right to give the wheat board an order to pay dues on behalf of farmers to farm organizations.
I realize it could be said, and might be argued, that if parliament authorized the holding of a plebiscite some basis would be given for the suggestion that we were favourable to the idea. I believe, however, that everyone understands that governments often hold plebiscites to ascertain the attitude of the people on certain matters, without the government having anything in mind beyond finding out the wishes of the people. The liquor question has been handled this way many times in different parts of this country. All this resolution says is that the wheat board should have the power to conduct a very cheap plebiscite amongst the permit holders to ascertain whether money in the hands of the wheat board should be subject to an individual's order that the wheat board turn over some of that money to pay farm union dues.
It will be noted that it is suggested that this plebiscite should be held by mail. The wheat pool delegates elect directors to run the business of the wheat board by means of a mail vote. The cost of conducting a plebiscite in this manner is very small indeed. It seems to me that when some farmers strongly hold the view that money in the hands of the wheat board should continue to be inviolate, not subject to attachment or assignment, and some farmers take the view very strongly that if farmers are going to maintain their position in our economy they should be given a chance to organize, and this is a way in which they could be assisted to organize, then we should give them a chance to decide whether or not it shall be done.
If this government were to introduce a change in the wheat board act and give the wheat board the power to conduct such a plebiscite, ballots could be sent to the permit holders and they could say whether they are favourable or unfavourable to this measure.


The farmers would then decide this matter. I say again, Mr. Speaker, that I am not suggesting the wheat board should be run by plebiscite. I am satisfied that at least 90 per cent of our farmers today believe the wheat board has done and is doing a splendid job of marketing their grain. The farmers do not want to do anything that would impair the efficiency of the wheat board as a marketing agency for their grain. If the farmers thought that such a move as this would in any way impair the efficiency of the wheat board or in any way weaken it, they would certainly vote against it. My submission is that the farmers themselves are the ones who can be trusted to decide whether or not it is the safe thing to do. After all, they are more concerned about the future success of the wheat board than members of parliament who are not farmers could possibly be. So far as this question is concerned, the future of the wheat board can be safely left in the hands of the farmers.
I submit that in asking members to support this measure they are being asked to uphold the idea of letting people run their own affairs as much as possible; that is all this resolution means. I am aware of the fact that some of my friends who strongly favour the check-off idea have pointed out to me that I voted against the idea of writing the check-off principle into law. I voted against it upon the understanding I got from the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gregg) that if the vast majority of the employees in an industry demonstrated they wanted the check-off they could get it written into a collective bargaining arrangement; that was the policy. It was a matter that should be left in the hands of the workers themselves, and not interfered with by parliament. I say that is the principle of this resolution, in the sense that the farmer would come under the policy of the government in regard to labour. If we want to have this right to have money in the hands of the wheat board available for assignment by the individual, and if he is to have the right to assign that money to pay farm organization dues, and if the farmers vote by a good majority in favour of that prooedure, then it means of course that the farmer can assign his money to pay those dues. It means there will be no cost upon those people who do not sign these assignments, because it has been said that the cost of operation will be taken out of those moneys ordered to be assigned.
So this procedure does not hurt the person who does not join. And it does mean that if a majority of farmers want to have this right, then they shall have it, just the same as people engaged in industry have a similar

right. I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that we should take the same attitude toward the farmers in giving them the closest possible approach to what is enjoyed by labour, where they have the right to make an order on their salary cheques or pay cheques. I believe this resolution oilers the closest approach by the farmer to that procedure, when it puts the matter in the hands of the farmers themselves, and lets them decide. That should be the privilege enjoyed by people under our system of government and, so far as is possible, having in mind the efficient functioning of the operation, the farmers should be permitted to decide for themselves.
I am not suggesting, let me repeat, that the wheat board should be run by plebiscite. But in this manner, after the wheat board has marketed the grain and has the money available, the farmers could be asked: "Do you, by a large majority, want to have the right to assign money only to the extent of paying farm union dues?" I suggest that this resolution is correct when it asks that the farmers be given the right to decide what should be done with the money received from marketing their own grain.

Mr. Speaker, perhaps it is a little unfortunate that I should be the first among my colleagues, and others, to rise at this time to state a somewhat different point of view. I think in the House of Commons we recognize that we can differ, and at the same time remain friends. I hope this instance is no exception.
I would refer first of all to the resolution. It may be considered that to a point what I am about to say this afternoon would be considered in the nature of technicalities. Nevertheless it is important to point out that the resolution suggests the taking of a ballot by mail of grain producers holding permit books.
Well, from my understanding of the permit book arrangement in connection with the delivery of grain, by no means all farmers hold such permit books. As recently as last fall I had brought to my attention cases where there were as many as five people interested in the production, sale and delivery of a certain block of grain, but only one of those persons had a permit. And in my own case, where I have a reasonable interest in a quantity of grain, I have no permit book. It is delivered in the other fellow's name.
So that this plebiscite to which reference has been made would not in any sense cover all those who are interested in grain. Of course we realize that difficulty could be overcome by taking a canvass of those who
Canadian Wheat Board do not have permit books. Perhaps in that way that objection would be overcome.
But I go further-and I think this is important, having in mind what was said by the hon. member for Rosthern (Mr. Tucker). It will be noted that the resolution refers to the payment of membership dues to farm organizations. Well, that is pretty broad. Does it include agricultural societies? Does it include 4-H clubs? How far down the line is this inroad to go, when being applied to the principle to which we have adhered in connection with moneys held by the Canadian wheat board? Perhaps this would be set out in whatever amendment might be proposed to the Canadian Wheat Board Act.
But the principle of the resolution goes beyond what I believe was in the mind of the hon. member who proposed it. I think we should know exactly what it means.
I voice my opposition to the resolution at this time-and I say "at this time" deliberately-in so far as it applies to the province of Manitoba-and again I draw attention to the words "as it applies to the province of Manitoba".
My main reason for doing so at this time is that we have in that province two farm organizations which for some time have been attempting to amalgamate, and to bring themselves into one organization. Up to now they have not succeeded, and I do not know whether they will succeed. But until that time is reached I do not wish to be on one side or the other, so far as those two organizations are concerned.
For my own part, let me say to the house that in my younger days I had a good deal to do with the activities of farm organizations. I was interested chiefly in the federation of agriculture, and the organizations which preceded it. But when one picks up a newspaper today he cannot fail to see the type of controversy going on between those two organizations in Manitoba. I submit we would be unwise to project ourselves into that controversy at this time, so far as that province is concerned.
The hon. member has brought up another point of view, which has been pretty strongly held, particularly by farmers delivering to the Canadian wheat board. I refer to the fact that up to now they have not wanted any procedure which would mean a prior claim on their money in the hands of the Canadian wheat board. The procedure set out in this resolution would be, I fear, the thin edge of the wedge. Once the principle is established, then claims of a similar nature and following the same principle might be made.
I know there are those who subscribe to the idea that the farmer should have the

Canadian Wheat Board right to have his membership dues collected by the Canadian wheat board. There are those who, improperly I suggest, look upon the Canadian wheat board as the employer with whom the farmer can negotiate and make a bargaining arrangement. The fact is, on the contrary, that the farmers have looked upon the wheat board as their employee. So it is not possible to work out a bargaining agreement in this respect between the Canadian wheat board and the farmer.
It may be urged that the taking of a plebiscite would be a reasonable approach to the matter, in that it would permit the farmers to say whether or not they want the adoption of this principle. But from everything I can gather it seems clear that the majority of farmers do not want it.
If in this instance we place the choice before them, then I think we are dodging a responsibility which we should accept in connection with declaring our attitude on this subject. But, even assuming the plebiscite is a reasonable approach, having in mind the controversy taking place in Manitoba now, it seems to me that the holding of a plebiscite would carry with it the implied direction that this is the desired procedure, and I am sure the holding of that plebiscite would influence many people in their votes.
In other words the government makes provision for the taking of a plebiscite asked for by one farm organization, and it would be assumed by a good many people that the government wants to lend its support to that organization. I do not think that is the case. I go further and I say this to you. You are asking the wheat board to conduct a plebiscite. It is true that the wheat board has the necessary documents, permit books and all the rest of it. But by so doing you are projecting the wheat board into a controversy that might do it more harm than good. If, in the wisdom of parliament, this step should be taken, then I suggest that a much more logical course to pursue would be to set up some other type of organization to take the plebiscite rather than the wheat board. I do not know what that would be; but I do subscribe strongly to the point of view that as far as possible the wheat board should be kept out of this thing which would inevitably become political one way or the other, and in the end it would do more harm than good.
I know that the argument of the hon. member for Rosthern (Mr. Tucker) is a very practical one. Having gone through that experience over a number of years I know some of the difficulty in collecting farm membership dues. I do not know whether it is reticence on their part, but the practical fact is that

owing to the sparse settlements it is somewhat difficult to collect the annual dues. Let me suggest this. If an easier indirect method is found, I feel that in the end it will do more harm to the farm movement than anything else could do. I believe that the farmers' movement will be successful and strong so long as it keeps active and virile within the various localities where it is established; and if farmers are strong adherents of their particular cause, they should come forward on their own to make their annual contributions of dues just as we do to our churches, clubs and other organizations. This reminds me that a few days ago I received a notice from an organization to which I belong. I thought my dues were paid but I received a notice that they were overdue for two or three years and that I should either put up or get out. Naturally, I responded.

As I understand it, Mr. Speaker, this resolution has been suggested in the first instance by the farm union movement of western Canada. In my judgment, up to the present time, this thing has not advanced to the point where I at least can subscribe to this principle. But that is not all, Mr. Speaker. taken in my own province of Manitoba to bring those organizations together in a strong grass-roots organization. That is possible if the leaders of the two movements will merge some of their differences and difficulties and recognize that the farmers themselves are the first essential.
I am reluctant to do this but nonetheless I think it is important. I refer to a radio broadcast that was made here not so long ago in which the leader of the farm union movement participated. It is important to have some knowledge of the point of view of some of these people. In this radio broadcast the then president of the farmers union was asked a question, and his answer was taken from the tape recording. I quote:

In so far as my own province of Manitoba is concerned, and believing in the principle, as I do, of people doing things for themselves that they can do for themselves, and having regard to the controversy that is going on in that province between the two farm organizations in that province, I must say that at this stage I do not propose to become a party to that controversy.

Canadian Wheat Board the purpose of keeping it that way I think I should put it on the record again. The resolution reads as follows:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should consider the advisability of empowering the Canadian wheat board to conduct a ballot, by mail, of the grain producers holding permit books to ascertain the wishes of such producers as to the wheat board complying with orders signed by such producers directing the wheat board to pay membership dues to farm organizations from money due such producers from the sale of their grain by the wheat board.
The first thing that comes to our notice on reading the resolution is that it is perfectly voluntary in its result.
As a matter of fact there are two distinct steps that have to be taken. In the first place, a plebiscite is to be carried out to ascertain the wishes of the permit book holders. If a majority of such permit book holders express the opinion that they do not wish such machinery to be set up, then of course no further steps would be taken.
The second and perhaps more important step is that the farmer concerned-I believe this is specified by the resolution-must request that his farm organization dues be deducted and handed over to the organization of his choice.
On this basis I can see no reason for the fears expressed by the hon. member for Portage-Neepawa (Mr. Weir) and certainly there are no difficulties in which the wheat board could get involved. The wheat board is not being asked to take sides in favour of one organization or another, or to advise the farmers whether they should ask that their dues be deducted or not. They are asked to do just one simple thing, to ascertain the wishes of the producers themselves. I see no reason why we should deny that simple request at this time.
I was not quite sure whether the hon. member who has just taken his seat was reluctant to support this resolution or whether he was opposed to it. In any event he did not express his support. His reason was that there was what he termed a controversy existing between the two farm organizations in Manitoba. I have no doubt that the hon. member has been in fairly close touch with the farm movement in Manitoba in the past and perhaps he still is, but to say that a controversy exists at this time between the two farm organizations in Manitoba is I think to exaggerate the picture quite substantially.
It is quite true that there are some differences of opinion in connection with the amalgamation of the two organizations, but I think we should be careful not to exaggerate the picture because the members of the one

Canadian Wheat Board organization, that is the Manitoba federation of agriculture and co-operation, are to a great extent also members of the Manitoba farmers union. That may sound strange as against what the hon. member for Portage-Neepawa has said, but it is a matter of fact.
The Manitoba federation of agriculture and co-operation includes all co-operatives. It so happens that I am a member of a consumer co-operative in my home town. I am not a farmer but by virtue of being a member of that consumer co-operative I am automatically a member of the Manitoba federation of agriculture. One can readily see how they would include the vast majority of farmers in Manitoba.
Then there are those farmers who have taken out membership in the Manitoba farmers union. By virtue of that they are already dual members, being also members of the federation of agriculture through their memberships in co-operatives. To say that these farmers are engaged in controversy would be to say that they are arguing with themselves because they are members of both organizations.
If there is a difference of opinion among some of the leaders of those two organizations, certainly this is the last place where it should be a surprise to anyone. We have differences of opinion here, not only as between one party and another but as between members of the same party. We have had an example of this in the last five minutes, but that is not something to be exaggerated into a controversy.
I have already pointed out that this is a perfectly good proposition. As a matter of fact the Manitoba farmers union and the interprovincial farm union council have already put themselves on record to make it clear that they are not asking the Canadian wheat board to do anything for them and that in fact they are willing to pay the expenses involved in having these deductions made and turned over to their organizations. Surely that is a fair proposition. I think they have gone a long way in making that voluntary offer to relieve the wheat board of the expense involved, which would not be great but which they feel the wheat board might object to paying.
What would be the effect if this resolution became legislation or if the wheat board were permitted to carry out the suggested plan? It would merely provide an orderly method of sustaining farm organizations. While mention has been made in several speeches of the farm unions, I think it should be made clear that the resolution is not restricted nor does it even specify farm union dues. It speaks of dues to farm organizations. In

other words, it is not designed to assist just the one farm organization. Its effect would be to help all farm organizations to which farmers wish to belong to carry out their activities in an organized and orderly manner.
Perhaps it would be useful at this time to mention some of the reasons why farm organizations exist and some of the values that they bring about. There are many, but I have picked out four which I think will commend themselves to all hon. members of this house. All farm organizations with which I have come in contact carry out educational work, and I mean educational in its broadest sense. They bring the farmers together into what we call locals or branches of the organization in various districts and by meeting regularly they carry out programs of an educational nature. Speakers are invited to come to give their views on various matters, not all of them dealing with agriculture.
They encourage the younger people who belong to take an active interest in what goes on around them, and again this is not restricted to agriculture. They want to help young farmers and farm wives to become good citizens. In that I believe they are doing an excellent job. For example, the 4-H clubs in Manitoba and the various locals of the farm union have in recent years carried out excellent educational projects which have helped to bring about a general level of understanding and participation, particularly among the younger people of the community. In that alone they are adding value to our society.
Then there is the question of research work. The various farm organizations have people who are asked to do certain research work for them, most of it being done on a voluntary basis. I have been often pleasantly surprised to find out how deeply informed in research matters were many men in various branches and how much excellent work had been done in that direction, in most cases without any remuneration whatsoever. These men are doing this work because they feel it is their duty to be useful to their fellow members.
Then there is the question of legislation. Time and again, either the government or members of the opposition propose certain legislation in this house or in the provincial legislature dealing with agriculture. I am quite sure that every hon. member would like to know the wishes and views of the farmers he represents on that proposed legislation. What better way to get an intelligent cross-section of opinion among farmers than by submitting the proposed legislation to these farm organizations for
[Mr. Zaplitny.l

their study, discussion and advice? That does not mean that in every case we must accept their views. We use our own good judgment about the thing. But in the meantime it is an excellent method by which the effect of that legislation on the producer can be brought out by the persons concerned who are on the ground floor.
I think the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) will bear me out in this. He will recall that not so long ago he was kind enough to pay a visit to my home town in connection with an official function he had to perform there. At that time he met with the executive of the local farmers' union. Although unfortunately the time was brief, it was not the minister's fault. He had to leave at a certain time but he was extremely generous with what time he had. They discussed certain problems. At that time I am sure he was impressed by the fact that here were farmers who were actually doing farming taking an interest not only in their own individual farms or in their own communities but in the agricultural policy of Canada as a whole and who were quite capable of discussing the matter intelligently with one of the ministers of the crown.
These things are valuable. They are valuable not only to the farmers themselves but to the government, whatever the government may be. It helps the government to have a better understanding of what the man who is doing the actual producing thinks, what he wants, what he considers is possible and desirable. That is another one of the values.
Then there is the social value. I remember a period of time in the province of Manitoba -and I am sure other hon. members also remember it-in which there was what I consider a deplorable lapse of time in which farmers were poorly organized, I was going to say; but in fact they were practically not organized at all. That period would be roughly between the time when the United Farmers of Manitoba ceased to be active and the time when the other farm organizations started again. There was a lapse of time there in which little was done in the way of farm organization. It is quite noticeable in those areas where farm organizations have again become active-both the Manitoba farmers union and the Manitoba federation of agriculture-where they have increased their activities, there has been a marked effect on the social life of the farmers themselves.
Mention has been made here of the fact that farmers are sparsely settled on the prairies. While we perhaps are not as widely scattered in my part of the province as they would be farther south or in some parts of 50433-864
Canadian Wheat Board Saskatchewan, it is true that it is not easy for the farmers to meet together socially; that is, it is not as easy for them as it is for those in the towns and cities. Here is one way in which they can come together regularly and not only give their attention to matters dealing with agriculture and the serious side of life but can meet in a social way, exchange ideas and have a pleasant evening together. I can assure hon. members that if at any time they were invited to attend a local meeting of the Manitoba farmers union or any other farm organization, they would have a pleasant evening. Such a meeting is not all seriousness and economic discussion; it is a social evening in the full sense of the word. That in itself is something that has a marked value in a rural community. It brings people together. They become better friends, better neighbours and better citizens in that way by participating generally in something in which they have common desires.
Those are some of the things to be taken into consideration. I certainly hope that hon. members of this house will accede to this request which is a reasonable one and a simple one. I want to support what was said by the hon. member for Yorkton (Mr. Castle-den) who preceded me. I hope it will not be regarded just as a matter to be taken under consideration, then shelved and forgotten. I hope the government will actively carry on with what is requested in this resolution if it carries in this house and, before too many months have gone by, will provide that machinery through which all the farm organizations may benefit by their individual members voluntarily asking the wheat board to perform this small service for them.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to say a word on this resolution, but I want to be brief. First of all, I want to congratulate the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Decore) on the manner in which he presented his case for his resolution this afternoon. I am sorry that I have to disappoint him and say that I cannot support his resolution as it stands because I think it is too general in some respects and too specific in others.

subtopic: ADVISABILITY OF BALLOT WITH RESPECT TO PAYMENT OF MEMBERSHIP DUES
speechtext: Then amend it and let us pass it.

speechtext:
It has been said that the resolution did not deal with the check-off as such. Of course, there are two definite aspects of this resolution. To begin with, the essence of the resolution itself is that it asks for a vote to be taken to ascertain the wish of the grain producers, to see whether they wish to have their dues to farm organizations deducted. But then, if
1344	HOUSE OF
Canadian Wheat Board the resolution is carried and if that is done, you have to face up to the check-off itself that will follow this resolution. Consequently it is rather difficult to envisage the vote without discussing the issue itself that will follow the vote should the vote be favourable.
My main objection to the resolution is that the Canadian wheat board is interjected into this vote. I should be pleased to see a vote taken to ascertain the wish of the farmers. Let me say this, however. I do not think the vote should be restricted to the grain producers. After all, we are dealing here with dues to farm organizations. What I am saying now probably applies more to Manitoba than to the other western provinces. For that matter, my constituency may be quite different from other constituences or other parts of western Canada. There is a large part of my constituency in which farm organizations are active, yet there are no grain producers in that entire area. If the vote is taken by the Canadian wheat board on that basis, it would mean that all these people would have no say in the matter. I suppose it can be said: "They do not have to have any say because even if the resolution carries, it is only the grain producers who will be able to deduct their dues. Whether the resolution is carried or not, they will not be able to have their dues deducted because they have no grain permit book and do not deal with the Canadian wheat board." That is one aspect of the resolution by which, when you ask the Canadian wheat board to hold a vote, you eliminate the non-grain producers from expressing their views and from the possibility of having their dues deducted later.
As has been mentioned by the hon. member for Portage-Neepawa (Mr. Weir), in a great many instances there is only one permit holder among four. In fact, I know of a case where there are five sons, for instance, in one family, each one having title to his own land, being the owner and operator of his own land, but on account of the fact that they use common machinery, only one permit can be issued to the whole five put together.

subtopic: ADVISABILITY OF BALLOT WITH RESPECT TO PAYMENT OF MEMBERSHIP DUES
speechtext: That is a bad practice.

subtopic: ADVISABILITY OF BALLOT WITH RESPECT TO PAYMENT OF MEMBERSHIP DUES
speechtext:
That is a general practice. As a matter of fact, everyone is fairly well aware of it, particularly since last year. We all know that last year, because the Canadian wheat board tried the unit system of delivery, the matter of who was the owner of the permit became a very live issue. There was a great deal of criticism and controversy throughout western Canada because naturally those who owned their lands


wanted their own permits. Situations such as these have come to our attention. I know that I have had many of them brought to my attention over the last year.
However, my main objection is that I hesitate very much to have the wheat board taking the vote. Frankly, the only reason the wheat board is asked to do it is that it appears to be more convenient. Over the years I have always taken the stand in the house that we should not burden the Canadian wheat board with any other responsibilities than the one of marketing grain. Because the board is doing a good job in a certain sphere, there is always a tendency to ask it to do more and more. There have been many occasions in the house since I have been a member when people have advocated that the wheat board should do this, that or something else. During the war there was a tendency to try to get the board to act as a price control agency. I remember many occasions when the view was put forward that here was a convenient organization which has a monopoly in the west and it would be very convenient to get them to do this, that and the other thing.
As we all know, the board, particularly at the present time, has more than it can handle in trying to dispose of the wheat crop, and to ask it to hold a plebiscite or vote at this stage may expose the organization to some criticism. As I have said, I have heard more criticism of the board in the last year than I have heard for a long time, and that disturbs me. To envisage placing the board in a position where it might run into even more criticism is disturbing to me. It is all very well to say that the board is not asked to take any part in the vote. All of us here have had some experience with elections and voting and, to say the least, I think it is a little naive to say that the board can hold a vote and not be involved in any way, shape or form in the vote itself.
I am not going to try to ascertain the degree of divergence of views existing between the two farm organizations in Manitoba. I think that even the hon. member for Dauphin (Mr. Zaplitny) will agree that there is some difference of opinion, and there are very great differences of opinion on the very issue that we are discussing now. I do not know what would happen, but I think it would be fair to assume that the one organization would take one stand and the other would take an opposite stand. Then you would have the Canadian wheat board in the middle. I do not think that would be to the advantage of the grain producers nor, indeed, to the advantage of the farm movement and the farm organizations themselves. We all want to see a strong farm organization.

speechtext:
I do not propose to re-fight the Selkirk by-election at this stage, but I know, because I went there and took part in the by-election, that this question was not an issue, and it is not because of it that the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Bryce) was elected. If the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue) was there, I am sure he will agree with that. I am not going into the other implications of the resolution. Indeed, a great deal would have to be said with respect to the actual application of the deduction of dues because that would require the amendment of the Canadian Wheat Board Act. I am sure that many people would have a great deal of compunction about any such amendment of the act, and the farmers as a whole would have to be told exactly what would be involved in the amendment of the act.
I do not think you could have a vote without considering fully what the result of the vote would be. If there were to be a vote you would have to discuss the whole question fully and put both sides of the argument before the people so that they would be in a position to decide either for or against. I do not intend to deal with this point at great
Canadian Wheat Board length, as a matter of fact not at all, except to say that if you do amend the Canadian Wheat Board Act to allow assignment then you will be opening the door. We might as well face it. It could be that the benefit to be derived from this proposal is worth the sacrifice of doing it. That is another question. However, so far all cheques going out from the wheat board have been, so to speak, sacred. No assignment whatsoever has been permitted. The board has had to deliver the money to the farmer and nobody has any prior right to it. When this provision was included in the act people were aware of what they were doing. It was done for a purpose, particularly at that time when there were so many after the farmers' money.
Times are a little better now and have been for some time, and the need is not felt now as much as it was in the past. The fact remains, however, that this provision is there, and when you say that you will make an exception for farm dues and allow nothing else you might as well face it that you are opening the door. If you amend the act to permit the wheat board to send money directly to any farm organization, then I know of another organization that will ask for the same privilege and has been asking for it for some time. I refer to the rural municipalities of western Canada.
They would very much like to have the money they advance to the farmers for seed grain deducted by the Canadian wheat board from the proceeds of the sale of the farmers'' grain. They have discussed this matter and they have asked for it. I am sure if we were to allow farm union dues to be deducted) these people would be right here to ask for the same privilege. It may be that the farmers would prefer to have it done that way, but that is another question. I say that the moment we open the door we have to face up to it that the provision preventing any assignment will disappear and we will have to take the consequences of such action.
However, that is the second stage, so to speak, and the vote has to take place first. I repeat that I would welcome a vote, but I am sure there must be other ways of ascertaining the views of the farmers on this matter. We ascertained the views of the farmers on the question of coarse grain, and I am sure other ways could be found of ascertaining their views on this matter. In the province of Manitoba I think that both farm organizations, and the Canadian wheat board particularly, would gain by waiting until the situation settles down a bit, until there is a merging of the two farm organizations and their views can be ascertained. It is true that some farm organizations have
1346	HOUSE OF
Canadian Wheat Board passed resolutions on this subject, but I do not know that the feeling of all members has been fully ascertained. I have not seen any resolution from organizations other than the farmers' union. I believe that would indicate that the farmers are not enthusiastic for this measure.
However, as I say, I am quite sure some other organization could be found to hold the vote. If it is quite evident then that the farmers would like to abandon the privilege they enjoy now under the Canadian Wheat Board Act and have their dues deducted, then we could study the possibility of doing so in the light of the circumstances at that time. I am very reluctant to draw the wheat board into this controversy. I do not believe the wheat board should be asked to conduct the vote; it should be some other organization.

subtopic: ADVISABILITY OF BALLOT WITH RESPECT TO PAYMENT OF MEMBERSHIP DUES
speechtext:
I thought this resolution had been so carefully worded by the hon. member for Vegreville that it had received the approval of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) and the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner). So far the speeches have run something like six in favour and two opposed, but it would appear now as though there would be some opposition from across the way. I would suggest to the hon. member for Portage-Neepawa (Mr. Weir) that the resolution is so worded that he should not worry even if he does not have a permit book. The resolution reads:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should consider the advisability of empowering the Canadian wheat board to conduct a ballot, by mail, of the grain producers holding permit books to ascertain the wishes of such producers as to the wheat board complying with orders signed by such producers directing the wheat board to pay membership dues to farm organizations from money due such producers from the sale of their grain by the wheat board.
This leaves the hon. member for Portage-Neepawa in the clear. If he has not a permit book he would be under no obligation if this resolution should pass. It would give those who have permit books the privilege of having some money paid to their own organizations from their accounts.
The hon. member for Provencher (Mr. Jutras) suggested that others who are not wheat producers should be consulted. I gather that he has in mind poultry producers or market gardeners in various parts of Canada.
I suggest to him that they are not involved. There is no reason why a poultry producer should be consulted as to whether or not wheat producers should be permitted to assign some of their funds to their own organization. If the other farmers want to devise a scheme
[Mr. Jutras.l

at any time so their dues can be paid by an easier method, they should be given support in this house.
The hon. member for Portage-Neepawa made a great deal of the argument that in the long run this sort of device would weaken the farm organizations. This has not been the experience of the trade unions. The same argument was used throughout the years as the trade unions sought to find a device to enable them to collect dues regularly without going to their members week by week or month by month. The trade unions in this country and every country have found that as they have improved their device for getting their dues they have been able to use their time for more constructive educational work.
I am sure anyone who has lived in a farm community will have a great deal of sympathy with the point of view expressed by the hon. member for Acadia, when he described the problems which arise when you go from farm to farm and find that a farmer is away at an auction sale, or is working on another farm, or he will be away until next week. The system used in Ottawa for collecting funds for charitable organizations by designating a certain night for the canvass is relatively simple. The canvassers can drive on paved streets in an area about the size of a township or a few townships in western Canada. If a canvass were undertaken to cover my constituency, 100 miles east and west and 500 miles north and south, where we have no paved roads at all, where we have not as many miles of gravelled road as we would like to have, and where we do have a great deal of rain, I think it is rather obvious that it would not be easy. It would be difficult to fix a date a month in advance or a week in advance and decide to cover a municipality or 10 municipalities on a given day or even in a given week.
I believe it is obvious that the proposal comes before us with a view to making it possible for farm organizations to get the funds they require by some economical method. This is a device used by other organizations without any argument. No one would suggest now that the trade unions should be asked to revert to a system whereby they would have to canvass their members each week, each month or each year for their dues. I see no reason why the privileges enjoyed by other groups in our economy should not be extended to the farm organizations. As long as I can remember the farmers in Canada as a group have not received a fair share of the national income. It is unfortunate that the farmers have not been able, during my lifetime, to build up a strong organization.

I am old enough to recall when Henry Ford introduced the $5 a day program into his plant at Detroit. At that time I was living in a Conservative part of Canada, and the farmers in Bruce county could hardly believe a man working in an automobile factory would receive $5 a day. It was thought this would certainly ruin the country in a very short time. It was not very long until Ford workers were going to their work in automobiles, and Ontario farmers thought that was a great calamity. They felt Canada should not be expected to provide automobiles so those making cars should be able to drive to work. I believe everybody would now admit that has been a good thing for Canada, to have workers, not only in automobile factories but in a great many factories, with incomes that enabled them to drive to work.
While organization has made it possible for doctors, lawyers and industrial workers to get a fairer share of the national income each year, the farmers have not been able to get together to build up their own organization so they could obtain a fair share of the national income. The member for Yorkton (Mr. Castleden) mentioned that in 1931 about one-third of the people in Canada were classified as farmers, and according to the last figures about 20 per cent were so classified. According to a bulletin of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture of April, 1954, the farmers' share of the national income is down to 8.7 per cent. I feel it is rather obvious that if 20 per cent of the Canadian people were organized they would not be accepting 8.7 per cent of the national income without doing something about it. I believe they could and would do something about it.
A bulletin of the federation of agriculture dated January of this year tells about the share of the Canadian dollar which is spent for various commodities. We are told that in the prairie region 23 [DOT] 3 per cent goes for food, 25 [DOT] 1 per cent is spent in the automotive world, 11-6 per cent goes for clothing and footwear, and 4-6 per cent for tobacco and liquor. I think it is obvious that when Canadians in western Canada spend only 23-3 per cent for food, there is something wrong with our economy. The farmers should have more dollars available so they could do a more effective public relations job, and take some action with respect to this 4-6 per cent for tobacco and liquor as compared with 23-3 per cent for food.
While the automobile is not a luxury for many people, the fact that 25 [DOT] 1 per cent of the dollar is spent in the automotive world while only 23-3 per cent is spent for food
Canadian Wheat Board certainly indicates that the farmers are not getting their fair share of the national income.
Looking through my files I found some figures concerning a self-propelled combine we bought to be used on our co-operative farm at Sturgis back in 1946. This was before the prices of combines went up to such fantastic levels. As the result of an error made at the factory the invoice for this combine was sent to us direct, instead of to Canadian Co-operative Implements, Limited, with their head office at Saskatoon. In other words the invoice we received showed the factory price at Brantford, Ontario. The price we paid for the combine was $3,421.35, while the factory price set out in the invoice was $2,308.25 or a difference of $1,113.10.
Some hon. members may say that the freight charges from Brantford to Sturgis would be very high. Let me reply that the freight charges were not nearly as high as we thought they would be. Two combines came down in one car for a total freight charge of $250, or $125 each. Take off the freight and there is still a spread of $988.10 between the factory price and the farm price at Sturgis.
Co-op Implements have done a pretty effective job in trying to narrow that spread, but it has not been easy for them to compete with the well-established firms such as Massey-Harris, International, John Deere, and other large corporations. I would stress the point that the $3,421.35 we paid gave the men in the farm implement factory an income so that they could support their unions; it gave the implement dealers an income to help maintain an effective organization, and gave the railway employees an income so they could support their unions. The only group that did not manage to get in on this deal were the farmers.
I think the proposal before us is very reasonable when it suggests that those who sell wheat should be given the chance to decide whether they would like to sign on the dotted line, instructing the wheat board each year to make payments to the union designated by the farmer. I cannot think of any good reason as to why the house should not support the hon. member for Vegreville in this reasonable resolution. The excuses advanced by the hon. member for Portage-Neepawa and the hon. member who has just taken his seat seem to me very lame indeed; and I am sure they would have difficulty in supporting those excuses before the people of their constituencies.
Just before the last election the interprovincial farm union council proposed an election manifesto for western agriculture in

Canadian Wheat Board
which a number of reasonable propositions were set out. One of these was the adoption of a voluntary requisition plan for the collection of farm union dues by the wheat board, through an amendment to the Canadian Wheat Board Act. I was asked whether I was for it or against it, and said that I was for it. I am sure all members from the rural constituencies in the three prairie provinces were asked to take their stand on this question. I hope those who were questioned before the election will not forget their commitments, and that they will support the hon. member for Vegreville in the resolution he has now placed before the house.
