speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: ADVISABILITY OF BALLOT WITH RESPECT TO PAYMENT OF MEMBERSHIP DUES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as a representative of an agricultural constituency I think perhaps I might be expected to say a few words at this time. In doing so, I should like first of all to congratulate the hon. member for Vegreville upon having introduced the resolution which has had the effect, until the present time- and I hope I shall not be the exception-of inspiring a debate which has been kept on a very high level indeed, and has been distinguished by an atmosphere of reasonableness in which the discussion has been carried on with a minimum of bias by members of all parties in the house. This is most desirable and in some measure almost inevitable in a subject of this nature, because I do not think there is any great amount of disagreement on most of the main points to be discussed. It is perhaps a question of emphasis rather than of outright differences of opinion that will determine our judgment.
For example I am sure no one would disagree with the hon. member for Dauphin in the stress he laid upon the vital importance of farm organizations. I remember with pleasure the incident to which he referred when I was in Dauphin, and I can only hope that the conversations we held at that time were as gratifying to the others who participated in them as they were to me.
Throughout the whole of my public life I have held the view that to the extent that farmers, and indeed all other occupational groups, combine together to take a close and intelligent interest in their own welfare, they make the work of public men easier; because it is then possible to conduct public business in an atmosphere of informed rather than uninformed public opinion.
Despite the fact that I represent an agricultural constituency, I would have hesitated to take part in the debate had it not been for the fact that up to the present time what has seemed to me to be the most important point in the discussion has been mentioned

only by the hon. member for Provencher (Mr. Jutras). To identify that most important matter we should ask ourselves first of all what it is that we are dealing with in this wheat board set-up.
I do not know of any better way of answering that question than by examining the statute under which it operates. If hon. members will do that they will see that section 25 of the Canadian Wheat Board Act states, in very clear language:
(1) The board shall undertake the marketing of wheat produced in the designated area in interprovincial and export trade and for such purpose shall-
And this is the first step they take:
(a)	buy all wheat produced in the designated area, offered by a producer for sale and delivery to the board-
And I shall not go into detail on that. Then, second:
(b)	pay to producers selling and delivering wheat produced in the designated area to the board, at the time of delivery or at any time thereafter as may be agreed upon, a sum certain per bushel basis in store Fort William-Port Arthur.
That is, they shall make cash payments. Then the next thing they do is:
(c)	issue to a producer, who sells and delivers wheat produced in the designated area to the board, a certificate indicating the number of bushels purchased and delivered and the grade thereof, which certificates entitle the producer named therein to share in the equitable distribution of the surplus, if any, arising from the operations of the board with regard to the wheat produced . . .
Thus it seems to me that the basic feature of this matter we are discussing is this. Ordinarily when moneys are held for and are payable to a farmer, they can be attached by garnishment proceedings. Moreover, the farmer can give orders upon them to pay certain creditors he wishes to prefer over others, and is often pressed by creditors to give such orders.
In order to avoid having farmers pressed by creditors seeking to get orders from him; in order to avoid having him harassed by garnishee orders issued by the courts of the country, to attach the moneys due to him, and in order to save the wheat board, which has a very difficult time indeed marketing the wheat produced in western Canada under the extraordinarily difficult world conditions today; in order to save this wheat board from accounting and other complications, it was provided in section 28 of the Canadian Wheat Board Act:
(1) The governor in council may, by regulation, (a) prescribe the form of certificates to be issued to producers delivering and selling wheat to the board, pursuant to section 25;

That is the section I read a few moments ago. I continue:
(c) prescribe the conditions under which the right to payment under a certificate issued pursuant to this part may be transferred.
Subsection 2 of section 28 is the crux of the whole matter. It says:
(2) Except as provided by regulation, no certificate issued pursuant to this part or the right to payment thereunder, shall be transferred or assigned, and no person other than the person therein named is entitled to payment thereunder and a statement to that effect shall be printed on each such certificate.
Why would they print that on each such certificate? As a notice to the farmer that in this wheat board certificate he had in his possession something which no creditor could attach, and in respect to which he could not even give an order to anybody that would have any legal effect.
The wheat board has carried on under these arrangements since its inception, and I believe that even amongst my friends of the opposition there will be general agreement- because I have heard them voice it on many occasions-that the wheat board under these circumstances has done a singularly good job. Among other benefits the farmers have had under wheat board marketings is the fact that they have been singularly free from harassment by their creditors in respect of moneys payable to them under those wheat board certificates.
My hon. friend can say well, that is all right, but if we have this plebiscite and if the farmers vote in favour of being permitted to sign orders upon the wheat board certificate moneys in favour of farm organizations, then what? That is what the resolution says. Many references have been made to the revocable check-off, and so on and so forth, but that is not what the resolution says and that is not what would be done. All the resolution we are considering says is this:
. . . complying with orders signed by such producers directing the wheat board to pay membership dues to farm organizations from money due such producers from the sale of their grain by the wheat board.
In other words the proposition here is that we should attack, and I would suggest destroy, the principle of the farmers' immunity from court process and pressure from his creditors in respect of these wheat certificates ... in order to do what? In order to save the farmer the trouble of putting his hand in his pocket and paying $5, or whatever the fee may be, to the farm organization of his choice.
I do not think that is a very good exchange.
I think it is a very bad one. And in support of my submission that this is a bad exchange I am going to proceed by analogy to the
Canadian Wheat Board argument made by the hon. member for Mackenzie who preceded me and who took his seat just a few moments ago. He is arguing in the house today, and those who supported this resolution have argued, that because the trade unions have had the revocable check-off therefore the farmers have just as great a right to a check-off of their own, and it should be extended to them. I am going to suggest that the immunity from process that the farmers of western Canada have enjoyed under the section of the act which I read to the house this afternoon is rather unique, and if we destroy that immunity to the extent of accepting orders in favour of farm organizations, I do not know upon what basis of moral principle we can deny to the municipalities the right to ask a farmer to give them an order covering the seed grain loan which they have advanced, or municipal hail insurance, or even their taxes themselves.

subtopic: ADVISABILITY OF BALLOT WITH RESPECT TO PAYMENT OF MEMBERSHIP DUES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as a farmer who has been active in farm organizations since I have been in Canada I should like to say a few words in regard to this particular problem. In my experience I have found that the greatest difficulty faced by farm organizations, as perhaps by other organizations, has been the matter of financing. This resolution has as its legitimate objective perpetuating
[Mr. Garson.1

their existence by finding a method of financing these organizations. We are living in an organized world. As everyone knows, organization is necessary to existence in that world. If it were not so there would be many fewer organizations than are now in existence.
Our lawyers have their bar association. I do not believe you can practise without being a member thereof. Often when I hear legal debates in this house I wish we could participate without being a member of the bar association. We also have medical associations and labour associations. Our bankers, our implement dealers, our butchers, our bakers, our candlestick makers are all organized. Everyone but the farmers in Canada are organized. This resolution is moved to help our farm organizations continue to exist. Their situation is entirely different from other organizations and, as I mentioned before, that is why this particular resolution is before this House of Commons.
Others have referred to the difficulty experienced by farm organizations in collecting dues as compared with other organizations. Just to illustrate, if a farm organization set out to interview the approximately 10,000 farmers in my constituency in order to collect dues they would have to travel a distance equal to one and a half times around the world. The money collected would never begin to pay the travelling expenses alone.
I appreciate that there will have to be some organizational work done in connection with the requisitions. It does not mean that the money is going to fall automatically into the hands of the farm organizations. They will have to go out among the farmers and organize for these requisitions which it will be necessary for the farmers to sign before their dues can be deducted. If we had the same control as is exercised by labour and professional organizations, if we could not farm unless we belonged to an organization, things would be different. But we as free people, as far as farmers are concerned at least, have to devise a different method of collecting our farm dues in order to remain in existence.
It is needless to refer to the benefits of farm unions. They are a necessity; they are absolutely essential in the scheme of things today. Not only have they brought about what we might call a new method of approaching farm problems within Canada, they have done much to bring about international unity. I think one of the greatest parts played by our farm organizations to the benefit of the economy of Canada was that part taken during the negotiations for the international wheat agreement. The vice-

president of our leading farm organization was there to advocate that the importing countries buying our wheat agree to pay on a cost of production basis so the farmers of western Canada could continue to produce that which is essential not only to our country but to all the world. Just in that sphere alone I submit that our farm organizations should be permitted to continue to exist.
There seems to be considerable feeling that the farm organizations are going to harm the economy of Canada. Nothing could be more untrue, because the objective of our farm organizations is to safeguard Canada. When the farming industry is safeguarded, then all Canada is safeguarded. The objective of our farm organizations is to make Canada prosperous and to keep it so. Mention has been made of possible political implications of farm unions. I think we can eliminate all fear as to our farm organizations operating politically.
We had some experience along these lines in western Canada for a number of years with the United Farmers. I can remember my wife and I driving 15 miles with a team of horses to attend meetings in the middle of winter because we felt this organization was trying to make our country more prosperous and a better place in which to live. But we all know the history of the United Farmers. They entered politics and they disappeared.
Our farm unions and farm organizations must be non-political. We need non-political organizations in Canada. There is not too much political unity west of the great lakes. Perhaps we cannot speak of unity west of the great lakes because of the various political theories and systems or whatever we may call them that we have in western Canada. So we need strong non-political farm unions. At times the people in the eastern part of Canada seem to indicate that they can get along without the people in western Canada. I want to see farm organizations which will spread the doctrine of unity in a non-political way so it will be acceptable to all the people of Canada, so we can be brought to that pinnacle where it will be possible to build a great united country. This is just not in existence in the west today in a political way.
We have been told that certain things will happen if a certain course is followed, but I do not think that is the point at all. The farmer who produces the grain markets that grain through his own organization. I contend that the wheat board is a co-operative, because it distributes at cost what the farmer produces and turns back to him what is available in value for his production and
Canadian Wheat Board work. The farmer as a member of that cooperative has certain rights. Mistakes may be made; but even if there are unfavourable, reactionary developments within the wheat board organization I submit it is still the farmer's right to vote as he wishes. It is a fundamental right and a human freedom that he should decide whether he wishes to have these deductions made. I think that is the only point we have to consider. Then if the farmer decides in favour of this we can take the next step.
I am not fearful, as some hon. members in this house appear to be, that this will destroy our wheat board, or bring about participation by others in the payments due to the farmer. I am not too greatly worried about that. I think the farmers will safeguard themselves. I believe all these things will be taken into consideration before the farmer casts his vote. I think he has sufficient perspective and wisdom to safeguard himself. All I wish to ask of the members of this house is that they grant the farmer that fundamental freedom we are all in favour of, the right to cast his vote. I believe everyone who thinks likewise will support this resolution.

speechtext:
We have had that point interpreted before, as my colleague reminds me. It is a resolution really directing the government to arrange that the wheat board take a plebiscite.
I am opposed to the principle of the resolution for several reasons, of which I should like to mention two or three. I am not going to weary the house by repeating the arguments that have been well stated by other hon. members who have spoken in similar vein. I will say at once that I have as high a regard for the co-operatives and the farm organizations of western Canada as any man in this house. There is every reason why I should have a high opinion of them, because I have worked with them now for the best

Canadian Wheat Board part of 35 or 40 years. When I was in private practice a good part of my income came from organizations of that type. I have a high regard for them, and I believe they have some regard for my opinions in matters relating to their activities.
If we arranged for the check-off I feel that it would not really be a favour to the farm organizations. I think the strength of every organization lies in that form of contact with the membership of the organization which comes through collecting their quarterly or annual dues. I have known other organizations which took that view. I know the railway organizations have only recently and in part come to the conclusion that they should have a check-off, either voluntary or otherwise. I have heard railroad men say they thought it would weaken their organization if there were not the kind of direct contact between the railway organizations and their members which comes from collecting dues whenever those dues are payable.
If this government undertook to arrange a plebiscite I think the implication would be that this government would look for a favourable outcome of that plebiscite. It has been pointed out by my*colleague the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) that the granting of a lien on the wheat cheque for the purpose indicated would break down all the immunities that are enjoyed by the producer in being free of deductions from his grain cheque. To me that is a tremendously important matter. If the principle of deduction, voluntary or otherwise, from the grain cheque were accepted, surely the collection of dues to farm organizations would not have the highest priority. There are many other priorities that would have to be considered. For instance, consider the seed grain which the farmer must have as a matter of necessity to put in his crop. Surely that payment would have a high rating for deduction from the grain cheque. Surely supplies the farmer needs to carry on his farming operations would have a place. If you were going to start making deductions from the grain cheque it would be only fair that the farmer should have the right of voluntarily electing that his payments for supplies be made deductible. Then there is the matter of municipal taxes. There is no reason why the farmer, if he can elect to have his dues deducted, should not arrange to have voluntary deduction of his taxes. A very wide door is being opened, and I think there is a great deal of danger entailed in the process.
Then there is the matter of loading this responsibility on the wheat board. If there is any board in this country today that has about all the obligations it is capable of carrying

out, I think it is the wheat board. They have had a difficult time. They have various problems apart from the selling of wheat. I see no reason why they should be elected first as the organization to test out the opinions of the farmers and then to collect dues for the farm organizations.
I have had it said to me many times, "We do not think it will carry, but why not have a plebiscite?" I am opposed to the idea that any difficult problem faced by the government should be settled by a plebiscite. After all, the electors of this country send us to their parliament to exercise our best judgment on their behalf and to make decisions in the light of the information we can obtain regarding their problems. I have heard candidates in election campaigns speak about plebiscites, particularly members of the Social Credit party. In their election literature that party suggested that they would hold plebiscites on various problems that were difficult to decide. I have never known of that party holding a plebiscite on any particular problem. In my nearly 20 years in this house I know of only one occasion upon which this government conducted a plebiscite as a guide to action to be taken. I am therefore opposed to the principle of the government sponsoring a plebiscite on this particular issue.
For the reasons I have stated, and for the reasons that have been advanced by my colleagues who have taken a similar view of this resolution, I shall vote against it.

He said:	When it became apparent last

In the first place I found, to my surprise, that there was little 1953 grain stored on the farms. Prairie Farm Assistance Act Of course this brought up the question of the Prairie Farm Assistance Act. Many farmers stressed the fact that the assistance that could be given under this act was not going to be sufficient to meet the needs.
Agriculture, Mr. Speaker, is the most important industry in Canada. It is subject not only to market conditions but to the many hazards of nature, such as drought, frost, wind, hail, floods, weeds, disease, insect pests, blights and so on. While other industries are able to a very large extent to buy insurance against hazards they may encounter, in most cases the farmer has to meet these hazards of nature without the protection of insurance. True, the grain grower can buy insurance against wind and hail, and since 1939 has had some relief under the Prairie Farm Assistance Act.
While I believe the benefits of that act should be extended to other parts of Canada,
I do not want to discuss that angle here this afternoon. What I want to do is point out the inadequacy of payments made today to farmers under the Prairie Farm Assistance Act. This act was put on the statute books in 1939, after eight crop failures. The purpose of the act was to provide farmers who had experienced crop failures with funds with which to carry on, and with those funds a farmer had to provide for his family and sow another crop.
1 Those who are responsible-that is, the government of that day-were not overly generous when they set the amount of the payments on which they thought the farmer could get along. At that time farm costs were comparatively low. Horses were the main motive power and were usually raised on the farm. Many farmers were able to grow enough feed for their horses, even though they had dry periods. Mechanization of the farms was only in its infancy, and farmers were able to use some of these P.F.A.A. payments to provide food and clothing for their families. Many of them could also secure wood for fuel, and it was a common sight to see strings of wagons going many miles to get their supplies of wood.
These conditions have radically changed. The horse has gone. Most farms are completely mechanized. Taxes have increased to two or three times what they were. Costs of production have skyrocketed while payments to farmers under P.F.A.A. have remained as they were in 1939.

subtopic: RESOLUTION SUGGESTING THAT PAYMENTS UNDER ACT BE DOUBLED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the house adjourned for dinner I had just placed on record a number of resolutions passed by different municipalities urging the government to double the payments to farmers under the Prairie Farm Assistance Act. I have more resolutions, but I do not intend to put them on record tonight. Later this month the rural municipalities association will be having their annual meeting, and I understand this matter is high on their agenda.
I said earlier in my remarks that when I made a survey of my constituency last fall I found quite a large number of farmers who had suffered crop failure in 1953. I have found since that this was the case not only in my constituency but throughout

the western provinces. In 1953 payments under the Prairie Farm Assistance Act were as follows:
Manitoba	 5,025	farmers
Saskatchewan	 5,733
Alberta	 5,547
16,305
That was the number of farmers who suffered a crop loss two years in a row. Those are the people who are badly in need of some cash assistance at the present time.
It is just as essential now as it was in 1939 that farmers who have had a crop loss or failure should receive sufficient assistance to carry them along. We all know that the wheat and grain grower, especially during the last ten or twelve years, has done more to put our economy in its present position than any other class. I should like to read a short editorial which appeared in the Ottawa Journal last week pointing out this fact. They say:
Last year was not a particularly good or happy one for prairie farmers. Largely by adverse weather and rust, grain crops were cut sharply, a lot of 1953 wheat still remained on farms or in storage, and the net result was that cash was none too plentiful in the three provinces. There was a substantial decline in farm buying.
This is bad for the prairies, but also for all of us. A survey just completed shows that in Canada last year 33 per cent fewer tractors, 64 per cent fewer combines and 44 per cent fewer threshers were sold than in 1953. In many cases farm machinery sales were lowest since 1944.
While a large part of our farm machinery sales are to prairie farmers the machines are almost all manufactured in Ontario. Ontario workmen were out of jobs because prairie farmers did not buy machinery in 1954, and they may still be out of jobs in 1955 unless things pick up on the prairies.
It's the old story of distant causes having their effect near home, something too often forgotten when the related questions of employment and agriculture are debated.
My whole argument is this. If $2.50 per acre assistance was needed in 1939, double that amount is needed today to provide the same assistance to the farmer.

subtopic: RESOLUTION SUGGESTING THAT PAYMENTS UNDER ACT BE DOUBLED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am happy to follow the hon. member for The Battlefords (Mr. Campbell), and I think he is to be congratulated upon bringing this matter to the attention of the house at this time. There is a certainty that this year the farmers of the prairie provinces have suffered an unprecedented crop failure due mainly to rust and the severe wet conditions which have prevailed in those provinces. The resolution moved by the hon. member reads:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should consider the advisability of introducing legislation to double the payments to farmers under the Prairie Farm Assistance Act.

This act was set up 16 years ago when the farmer's cost of production was much lower than it is today. Since that date the act has never been changed to increase the payments; consequently when payments are made in all fairness they cannot be said to meet the needs of the farmers. The farmer's cost of production has risen greatly in the years since 1946. The house will recall that controls were taken off by this government shortly after the war, and it was not very long before the farmer's cost of production began to rise, especially the cost of farm machinery. In some cases farm machinery prices have increased 150 to 200 per cent over what they were prior to 1945.
Today the farmer finds himself in a cost-price squeeze, a position about which he can do very little as far as reducing his cost of production is concerned. In the three western wheat-producing provinces crop failures have made it very difficult for the farmers to carry on. Looking at the consolidation of the Prairie Farm Assistance Act I find that section 3 is entitled "Crop Failure Assistance".
The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) has indicated to the house that the act was set up primarily to meet drought conditions. It may be quite true that that is what they had in mind at the time, but I see nothing in the act which would prevent it being used to cover other types of crop failure. I plead with the minister and the government to do everything possible to make this problem easier for western farmers who have suffered such severe losses from crop failures due mainly to rust and wet conditions.
Many sections of the west were flooded. In some sections farmers were not able to put in crops and in other sections where they were able to put them in the continuous rains were so heavy that they had absolutely no crops. Then we suffered from stem rust, called 15-B, which took a great deal of our western crop.
I am sure all hon. members of the house want this act to be as comprehensive as possible so it will carry out its objectives. I was able to spend a few days up in the interlake country of Manitoba helping my good friend the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Bryce), and they told me there was a large section of country which was not covered by the act. Having regard to the position and the plight of the farmers up there, I want to appeal to the minister to do something about that condition so these people will have coverage under this act. They have been paying their share, by the deduction provided for in the act, of 1 per cent levied on the return from their grain. I think it only fair that they should also have the payments, but according
Prairie Farm Assistance Act to the act they are not eligible. I do not think that under the act as presently constituted they are getting a fair deal.
I should like to draw the attention of the house to chapter 213, section 3, subsection 2, paragraphs (ii) and (vi). There we find that in special areas where the settlement has been made under the Veterans Land Act they are now eligible for payment, but I understand there are still sections which, by agreement between the federal government and the provinces, are not covered under the act. Then too we have large blocks of land which again were formerly provincial lands, which were classified as marginal or submarginal but later were found to be productive when brought under production. Today grain is being produced on many sections of land of that nature. I would plead with the minister to change the act so these sections will be brought under its terms.
I have stated something of the plight of western farmers, and I think it is unnecessary for me to repeat the arguments or the statistics which were given previously by the hon. member for The Battlefords. I believe it is sufficient for me to say that the net Saskatchewan farm income dropped from $473 million in 1953 to $111 million in 1954. Those figures are for the calendar years. Furthermore, since 1951 the prices of farm products have dropped 22 per cent while production costs have gone up 16 per cent.
One can readily see the plight of the farmers, even those who were fortunate enough to have good crops again this year. But I happen to come from the constituency of Moose Mountain, which is situated in the southeastern portion of the province. It is perhaps one of the hardest hit areas in Saskatchewan this year owing to flooding conditions and the 15-B rust. I would therefore plead with the minister to do something about the situation existing in those areas where the act does not now cover the farmers.
On February 17 I asked the minister the following question, as recorded at page 1237 of Hansard:
Mr. Speaker, has the minister's attention been drawn to the situation where small acreages of Selkirk wheat have disqualified farmers from payment under the Prairie Farm Assistance Act? Can the minister state whether in all cases Selkirk wheat will not be a determining factor in deciding eligibility under that act?
The minister's reply was as follows:
On two or three occasions at this session I have announced to the house that, prior to the seeding period of 1954, the government had distributed Selkirk wheat to quite a number of farmers in Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta. They distributed six bushels to farmers who seeded it on

Prairie Farm Assistance Act from two to three acres, and have grown crops from it. None of the crops grown as a result of that distribution has been allowed to influence in any way the decisions with regard to payments under the Prairie Farm Assistance Act in those areas. In other words they are not allowed to prevent payment in the area because of that particular production.
I have tried to make a survey in my constituency, and I have found to date there has been a great deal of indecision with respect to whether or not payments are going to be made. I want to read to the house a portion of a letter forwarded to me by a constituent who had received it from the department of agriculture at Regina, the P.F.A.A. branch. It reads in part as follows:
In view of the small acreage of wheat with a high yield we had already determined to take this block back to the board of review to be reconsidered. We cannot prophesy just what their decision will be and, therefore, hesitate to make any hopeful prediction.
The letter goes on to say that they are going to have the matter under review. My appeal to the minister is that in all cases in determining eligibility under this act Selkirk wheat should be taken out of consideration and that, regardless of what acreage a farmer may have, it should not in any way disqualify the remainder of his farm should he have other acreage under production, nor should it disqualify any block of sections which otherwise would be eligible under the act.
I think this can be done without any contravention of the act and without any changes in the act. In the regulations, chapter 213, section 5, we find paragraph (e) which reads as follows:
(e) providing that in special circumstances another kind of grain may be taken in lieu of wheat as the basis of awards under this act, and in that event what number of bushels of such other kind of grain shall be deemed to be equivalent to a certain number of bushels of wheat for the purposes of such substitution;
If the minister is willing to do so, I think he can rule out, under the regulations, wheat in certain areas as the qualifying grain for eligibility, and can accept the farmer's production of coarse grains. Then again in the same section, in paragraph (g) we find this provision:
(g) excluding from the operation of any section of this act any lands in the spring wheat area and any grain grown thereon;
I think that paragraph makes it quite clear that this year, without waiting for any amendment to the act, these people can be covered so they will not suffer through having no payment under this act.
I might point out to the minister that many of the farmers in my constituency last year- that is in the crop year 1953-suffered conditions of rain and flooding as a result of which
fMr. McCullough (Moose Mountain).]

they had little crop. This year the situation is just doubly hard because it is the second year in a row during which many farmers in my constituency have lost their crops. Consequently merchants are in need of money. In many cases the municipalities are not able to collect taxes. The problem is urgent.
Of course I think the government has been remiss in the past in allowing the decontrol of prices to put the farmer into the present position. While it is true that we had for three years-namely 1951, 1952 and 1953- abnormally large crops, the fact remains that the indebtedness of western farmers has increased both under the Canadian Farm Loan Act and under loans from the chartered banks. Therefore I appeal to the minister to take what I have said into serious consideration and make these payments.
There is one other thing I wish to say in closing. I think the government has been remiss in not doing something about this matter earlier. The crop was taken off some three months ago. The act stipulates that the first of these payments should be made about December, the second 40 per cent being in the month of March following. I think the government should speed up these payments so the farmer will have at least this payment in order to meet some of his current expenses.

subtopic: RESOLUTION SUGGESTING THAT PAYMENTS UNDER ACT BE DOUBLED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the resolution before us has caused me considerable concern, because I have been interested in the Prairie Farm Assistance Act for a good many years. I have been convinced that the act has provided a good many farmers in Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta with considerable benefit over the last 15 years, helping them in their farming operations. But the act is now 15 years old, and since it was made law in 1939 a good many changes have taken place. Conditions today are much different from those of 1939 which the act was supposed to be designed to meet. The act has not been amended to keep pace with the changes or the needs of these times. We think it is time for a thorough overhaul of the legislation to bring it into line with the realities of the present situation.
The hon. member for The Battlefords made what I thought was a good case for increased payments to the farmers under the act. His main argument, as I heard it, centred around the increase in costs to the farmers since 1939 or, if we want to put it another way, the serious decline in the purchasing value of the Canadian dollar since 1939. I think that argument is valid; but at the same time I suppose we would have to admit that the government's argument will also be valid,

namely that the dollars contributed by the farmers to the fund are also short in purchasing value.

subtopic: RESOLUTION SUGGESTING THAT PAYMENTS UNDER ACT BE DOUBLED
speechtext: That is all the more reason why the payments should be increased.

subtopic: RESOLUTION SUGGESTING THAT PAYMENTS UNDER ACT BE DOUBLED
speechtext:
But at the same time I think the government might argue that if the benefits under the act are to be doubled, then the farmers will also have to consider doubling their contribution because there is no fund that has accumulated over the years. We have to admit the validity of that argument. But does that mean to say for one moment that increased payments should not be made to farmers under the act.
There is a good deal of dissatisfaction expressed with this act and its administration. As I go about my constituency and other parts of the country I have discovered that the farmers generally are just not pleased with it, and there are several reasons they cite. One has to do with the way the government interprets the definition of the word "farmer" as it is set out in section 2, subsection 1 (e). In so many cases we find that the word "farmer" is interpreted in such a way as to do a valid farmer out of his benefits under the act even if he should qualify in the township.
For instance, take the case of a man who has been forced by the circumstances of the times, that is a minor recession or something of the kind, to find a job to supplement his meagre farm income. Nevertheless he does go ahead, farms his land and tries to be a good farmer as defined in subsection 1 (e) of section 2 of the act. But when at the end of the year he finds that his whole township or area qualifies for payment under the act and he makes an application, he is denied the benefit because it is said that investigation shows that he has received a little more than 50 per cent of his income for the year from a pursuit other than farming.
That interpretation has been used in many cases to deny bona fide farmers the benefits of the act, and the people generally are not satisfied with that situation. They feel tnat because over a good many years they have contributed to the fund out of which the benefits are paid they should be entitled to the benefits if in their farming operations the crop yield falls below the 8 or 4 bushels per acre prescribed in the act.
That is only one of many complaints. I find that there are ,a good many farmers in different parts of the country who are unhappy over the operations of section 6, particularly subsections (a) and (b). Many injustices have been caused, and the application of these clauses has been very unfair. I think section
Prairie Farm Assistance Act 6 (c) was very good initially, but sections 6 (a) and 6 (b) certainly can be and are used by the administration to bring unfairness and injustice to many farmers.
In Alberta particularly crop loss very often results from hail. The administrators of the act do not like to admit that hail loss is a cause for benefits to be paid under the act, but it is admitted that where hail loss causes a drop in yield to below 8 bushels or 4 bushels to the acre, if the whole area in which their farms are situated qualifies the farmers are to be paid the benefit. Amongst the farmers in hail districts much dissatisfaction arises because of the fact that the hailstorm may sweep over a particular area totally destroying the crop, but the area will not be large enough to qualify for benefits. It may also be that the small area totally destroyed is in an area of otherwise very high yield, and so the operation of section 6 (c) is denied.
Because of the fact that this does happen so often in high production areas, and injustice occurs, we feel that it is not merely a question of increasing the payments to farmers. That would of course meet the needs of a good many farmers who feel that this year they are in need of emergency assistance, as has been suggested by the mover and seconder of the resolution. But that is only part of what we think should be done with the act. We believe it is time for a complete overhaul of the legislation. We are not against what the mover of the resolution is seeking to achieve. We support the need for higher payments, and we do not want what we are about to propose to be interpreted to mean that we are opposed to the resolution itself. We shall support it, but first we would like to test something else by way of an amendment to the resolution. I move, seconded by the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Quelch):
That the resolution be amended by deleting all of the words in the third and fourth lines thereof and substituting the following therefor: "(1) referring the Prairie Farm Assistance Act to the standing committee on agriculture and colonization for a thorough study of the administration of the act and (2) amending the Prairie Farm Assistance Act to establish the basis of qualification for payments of benefits on an individual farm basis".

speechtext:
Whatever may be the position of the amendment itself, Mr. Speaker, perhaps just proposing it suggests the sort of thing that is in our minds. We do feel it is not enough merely to ask for an increase in the payments. I suppose such an increase would materially help those farmers who this year find themselves in a bad position as a consequence of the widespread crop failure last year, and who could qualify under the act. But it would not help those people who have been on the borderline, or who cannot now qualify as a consequence of the interpretations that are placed on some of the definitions as well as through the operations of section 6, subsections (a) and (b).
It seems to me that the only way we can get down to something like a complete overhaul of the act to bring it into line with today's needs is to have it brought before a committee for study. I would suggest that the government do that of its own motion, without having it called for from the other side. No one can argue that after 15 years of operation, with only minor amendments here and there, the act does not need to be brought up to date and does not need a thorough overhaul. We suggest that instead of amending it piecemeal, we bring in amendments that will be really worth while. I suggest, too, that we should bring this Prairie Farm Assistance Act more into the category of an insurance program. I feel that is what we thought it was going to develop into. I suggest the farmers themselves had every reason to believe that the Prairie Farm Assistance Act, as passed in 1939, would gradually develop into a worth-while crop insurance program.
I suggest that the government give very careful consideration to subjecting the act to a thorough study and overhaul. In our judgment it is the only way a satisfactory result could be obtained. We shall support the request of the hon. member, because we do feel that increased payments should be


made; but at the same time we would not feel that that is as far as we should go.

subtopic: RESOLUTION SUGGESTING THAT PAYMENTS UNDER ACT BE DOUBLED
speechtext:
I have already indicated my thoughts as to the consideration that should be given to increasing these prairie farm assistance payments, in my speech on the address in reply to the speech from the throne. I do not intend, therefore, to take up too much time tonight, other than to mention again some of the points to which I feel the government might give consideration.
As has been pointed out, when the act was first passed in 1939 the average price the farmer received for wheat was about 57 cents per bushel. With the 1 per cent deduction he was paying to the government a little over half a cent or -57 cents per bushel. The average price the farmer has received for No. 1 northern wheat during the last eight years has been about $1.63 per bushel. In other words, for eight years the average amount collected by the government under this 1 per cent deduction has been 1 [DOT] 6 cents per bushel, or roughly three times the amount per bushel that was collected when the act was first passed. By virtue of the increase in the price of wheat, due to some extent I suggest to a drop in the value of money, the amount collected by the government has been increased but the amount a farmer can collect has not been increased.
The figure to which most reference has been made is the maximum amount a farmer can receive, namely $500. Some hon. members might be under the impression that in a year of crop failure the farmer will get $500. In order to get $500 there has to be 400 acres under crop, which would mean that the farmer would have to have at least three-quarters of a section. So there are literally thousands of farmers who have no hope of qualifying for the $500 maximum payment. This year, when a great many farmers have had almost complete crop failure, the average payment under the Prairie Farm Assistance Act, which was designed to help tide the farmer over to the next harvest and help him seed his crop, will be somewhere between $200 and $250.
On the basis of the cost of living back in 1939, $200 is worth less than $100 was then. As has been pointed out, the farmer's cost of production and cost of living, on the basis of 1935-1939 equalling 100, have now risen to 225. In other words it takes $225 to do the same work in helping tide the farmer over the year and put in another crop that he could do with $100 in the days when the act was first passed.

I submit, Mr. Speaker, we have recognized that money does not go as far as it did some years ago in regard to other occupations. We have recognized it by raising our own salaries; we have recognized it by raising the salaries of civil servants. We have recognized it all along the line by doubling pension payments and increasing unemployment insurance payments. It has been recognized that a dollar does not go as far as it would 15 years ago. Since for the past eight years the farmer has been paying into this fund about three times as much per bushel as he was when the act was passed, since the money he is getting back is worth less than half in so far as purchasing power is concerned and doing what the act was designed to do, then it seems to me a case has been made out for considering increasing these payments.
It has been pointed out that the government has paid out to our western farmers about $146 million under this act, and under the 1 per cent deduction provision they have collected slightly less than $80 million. The government has, therefore, paid out of the consolidated revenue fund about $66 million.
It has been recognized that the only reason we can grow hard wheat in our prairie provinces is because it is a more or less semi-arid region. It was recognized also that the government had a choice of either paying out agricultural assistance during the future years of crop failure or setting up a scheme to which the farmer would contribute but which would not be self-supporting. Repeated studies of the situation in western Canada and in similar parts of the United States have shown that the areas that need this protection most cannot afford to pay a sufficiently high premium to provide crop insurance. It was realized from the outset that the government would have to contribute to any scheme that would substantially alleviate these conditions.
In 1939 it was considered better for the government to set up a scheme to which farmers would contribute, facing the fact that from time to time the government would probably have to contribute to the fund to make up any deficiency. That fact was faced by the government of the day; and at this point I wish to pay tribute to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) for introducing the measure and having it accepted by the House of Commons. I was present when he did this, and I would say to him that this legislation has been greatly appreciated. I am sure it will be appreciated in future, and I hope the Minister of Agriculture will be with us for many years to witness its application.
This act has been of such great assistance to the farmers of western Canada that I am
Prairie Farm Assistance Act sure the work of the Minister of Agriculture in this connection will be appreciated for a long time to come. Those of us who are taking the position that the payments should be increased are simply saying that the act should be placed in a position where it would give assistance to farmers to get them over a difficult period, until the following year, so they may look after their families and sow their crops. For this purpose we feel that the payments should be as effective today as when the act was passed.
When we ask for this I submit we are not asking for anything that is really out of place. At the time the act was passed the millions of dollars it was contemplated would have to be put into the scheme bulked much larger, when compared with expenditures by the federal government at that time, than would a similar amount today. Hon. members will recall that at the time the act was passed total expenditures by the federal government were in the neighbourhood of $400 or $500 million, and of course they are much greater today. If at that time we were ready to face an expenditure considered so worth while, then I submit we should bring the act up to date, when the amount involved represents a much smaller proportion of total national expenditures.
It has also been repeatedly brought to my attention-and members from the prairies will realize that this is correct-that these payments are made to individual farmers. The maximum amount payable is $500. In other words the act was designed to help the small farmer. No matter how big a farmer's operations may be, he cannot get more than $500 under the act.
The trend in western Canada has been such as to reduce the possible obligation of the federal government under the act. In 1941 there were 298,131 or almost 300,000 eligible farmers in Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta and the Peace river area. In 1951 the total number of farmers who might conceivably qualify for help under P.F.A.A. had decreased to 250,302. In other words the number of farmers who might hope to get benefits under the act had decreased by 47,829 in the ten-year period between 1941 and 1951. This means a reduction in the amount the national treasury would have to face in the event of total crop failure. It has been pointed out that since that reduction in liability has taken place, it would be even more in order to bring up the purchasing power of the amount paid under the act to where it was when the act was first passed.
Something has been said by some of my friends about our being too much inclined to ask for help from the national treasury. Let
1382	HOUSE OF
Prairie Farm Assistance Act me point out to members in all parts of the house that when western Canada is prosperous the whole of Canada tends to be prosperous. Depression struck first in the thirties in the agricultural areas of Canada, the prairie areas; and it would not be a good thing now for the national economy to permit the purchasing power of the western prairies to sink too low. That was one of the original ideas behind passage of the act, to tide the west over those times it had crop failures, which it was recognized were bound to occur from time to time. It was considered better to have a scheme like this to maintain purchasing power in days of crop failure, not only from the standpoint of helping out the farmers but also from that of lightening the blow to the national economy.
I submit that if payments under the act are increased, as I suggested during the debate on the speech from the throne, or if they are doubled, as is now suggested, it might cost the government about $25 million more. This amount would go into circulation, with the result that it would build up employment here in central Canada and, generally, prevent as much suffering from a crop failure. It would do just as much good in central Canada as it would in the west, because everyone knows that most of the money paid to our farmers is ultimately used to buy goods produced here in central Canada. So I suggest that if this scheme were amended so it could do what it was intended to do originally, not only would it help us in the west but it would help the economy of Canada as a whole.
One of my reasons for taking part in the debate is, as hon. members know, that last fall our party had a convention in Saskatchewan. I believe I am quite within the mark when I say it was one of the most enthusiastic and best attended political conventions ever held in the history of our province. At that convention a resolution was passed asking the government to give consideration to increasing payments under the act. This was one of the measures which made me proud of supporting the Liberal government of that day, which passed this act which has been of so much benefit to the people on the prairies. And I take equal pride in supporting the government now in office which has improved the act from time to time. I am quite satisfied consideration will be given to the representations for further improvement made from time to time. It seems to me a good case has been made out for increasing these payments this time.
I went over these points in my speech in the debate on the address in reply. Since


that time I have received more mail concerning that speech than I ever received with respect to anything I have said in the House of Commons. In that mail were resolutions from eight municipalities in and around my constituency. I have received representations from wheat pool committees, from farmers' union lodges, and from individuals. I have received letters and petitions, and there is no doubt that the farmers of western Canada, knowing that this government passed the act in 1939 and knowing also that it does not go as far as it did when it was first passed, have great confidence that favourable consideration will be given to the request for increased payments.
I commend the government most highly upon having passed the act originally, and in particular I commend the Minister of Agriculture upon his leadership in that direction. I look forward with confidence to this matter being given the consideration I feel it deserves.

speechtext:
I think I should dispose of the amendment moved by the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Low). It is not without hesitation that I do so, because the hon. member and I seem to be always at variance recently. Latitude on private members' day is quite wide. Although in the discussion of the subject matter of the resolution moved by the hon. member for The Battlefords (Mr. Campbell) great latitude is allowed, when it comes to amendments one must be very careful because otherwise they may be used as precedents, and if we should let one go we do not know where it might take us.
Probably the hon. member has read citation 344 of Beauchesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms, third edition, and has construed the citation and the resolution to mean that provided he was dealing with the Prairie Farm Assistance Act he was on the subject matter of the motion and therefore his amendment would be relevant.
What is the subject matter of the resolution moved by the hon. member for The Battle-fords? It is not the Prairie Farm Assistance Act. He wants an amending bill to double the payments to farmers under the Prairie Farm Assistance Act. Therefore the subject matter is the doubling of the payments, and any amendment moved would have to be relevant to that particular subject matter, the doubling of the payments.
What the hon. member proposes in his amendment is a totally different subject matter which could be the substance of a motion moved after notice and debated in this house under the heading: "Notices of Motions".

He proposes to refer the Prairie Farm Assistance Act, the entire act, to a standing committee and amend it in a particular different from that which is being asked for by the hon. member for The Battlefords. It has no reference to the doubling of the payments. He wants to amend it in order to establish the basis for payment of benefits on an individual farm basis.
If he reads citation 344 he will see:
It is an imperative rule that every amendment must be relevant to the question on which the amendment is proposed. Every amendment proposed to be made either to a question or to a proposed amendment should be so framed that if agreed to by the house the question or amendment as amended would be intelligible and consistent with itself.
The law on the relevancy of amendments is that if they are on the same subject matter with the original motion, they are admissible but not when foreign thereto.
The amendment of the hon. member relates to the Prairie Farm Assistance Act but not to the doubling of the payments under the act, and that is the distinction. Therefore, with much regret, I must rule the amendment out of order on the ground that it is not relevant to the subject matter of the main motion.

subtopic: RESOLUTION SUGGESTING THAT PAYMENTS UNDER ACT BE DOUBLED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to congratulate the hon. member for The Battlefords on the very important motion he presented this afternoon for the consideration of the house. The Prairie Farm Assistance Act is of very great importance to western Canada. It is an act, as hon. members have said, that has been on the statute books since 1939. It was placed on the statute books by a Liberal administration. No one in this group is attempting to withdraw from the Liberal administration any credit that is theirs because in 1939, after they had been in office for four years, at long last they did something that would provide an alternative to the relief that was being distributed in those days.
Do not let anyone in this house go away with the impression that in this act we have something peculiar to western Canada; that it is one of those things, as so many hon. members like to believe, that is intended to benefit western Canada only; because if hon. members will study other acts of this government they will find that from 1948 to 1953 the government provided the gold mines of this country with a subsidy of $65 million. This amount is almost as great as the subsidy of $66,400,000 paid over a period of 16 years under this act, for the benefit of over 200,000 farm families on the prairies. Therefore I say in relation to the treatment given the gold-mining companies, the treatment given
Prairie Farm Assistance Act western wheat producers has not been any great credit to the government.
The Prairie Farm Assistance Act came about, as I have said, because of the huge relief bills paid in the 1930's, owing to low farm prices. That is the main reason, but there was also the fact that there were many years of lower than average crops. According to the book entitled "The Wheat Economy" by Professor Britnell of the University of Saskatchewan, between 1929 and 1938 the dominion government paid out in relief, or had guaranteed provincial payments, a total of over $131 million in the province of Saskatchewan alone. It was in the light of the calamity that results from widespread crop failures that this act was placed on the statute books. It was put on to make sure that such relief payments would not have to be made again.
Along the same lines and for the same reason the government placed on the statute books the Unemployment Insurance Act. I as a member of the C.C.F. party am very happy indeed that we have the Unemployment Insurance Act. We would like to see its benefits extended and the act improved. It should be pointed out that under that act the government has already contributed, in a shorter period than the Prairie Farm Assistance Act has been in existence, the large sum of $248 million. I repeat, the moneys paid out of the federal treasury toward prairie farm assistance are not payments made peculiarly to western Canada, because other acts have provided for payments to other sections of the economy.
If any hon. member in this house from Ontario, the maritimes, Quebec, British Columbia or any other place wishes to say something about this act I suggest that instead of making any criticism of the Prairie Farm Assistance Act and the moneys the government has paid out under it, he should be standing in his place fighting on behalf of the producers in those provinces for the same kind of protection, in the event of a crop failure, that the prairie farmers have under the Prairie Farm Assistance Act. If the members who have tobacco growing areas, potato growing areas or fruit growing areas or other such areas in their constituencies would rise in their places in this house and support improvements in this particular measure, and join with us in asking that the provisions of such an act be applied to all parts of the agriculture industry, they would be doing a whole lot more for their own provinces and for agriculture than they would by criticizing the benefits that have been paid under this act.

Prairie Farm Assistance Act
I listened very carefully to the speech delivered by the leader of the Social Credit party and I failed to see why he should in any way criticize or wish to amend, even by way of suggestion, the motion moved by the hon. member for The Battlefords asking that the payments be doubled. Instead of supporting such a motion he wants to amend it by deleting the most important part of it. He does not want to improve the act by making additional payments; he wants the whole question of the administration of the act referred to the committee on agriculture for study. Prairie producers are 100 per cent in favour of the resolution to double payments moved by the hon. member for The Battle-fords. They are not asking that this motion be studied; they are asking that the government take action along the lines suggested in this resolution.
Since I have been in this house, from 1945,
I have seen the government adopt suggestions made from this side of the house which brought about improvements in the administration of the act. I have seen the act amended time after time so that payments were made on a somewhat smaller area. As far as I am concerned, while I am criticizing the act itself I have little or no criticism to offer of the detailed administration of the act. In any cases I have brought to the attention of the officials of the Prairie Farm Assistance Act, while I may not always have obtained the answer I would have liked to obtain, I almost invariably received a fair decision related to the provisions of the act. Therefore I cannot join with those who have complained about the detailed administration of the act.
However, I support the request that the area on which a payment is made should be reduced. Over the years the trend has been in that direction, and it should be continued. At the present time payment may be made on a half township. After a half township has been established, payment may be made on a one-sixth township if it is a rectangular area with one side lying alongside an eligible township. I should like to see the six-section block reduced to four sections, to two sections-yes, right down to at least one section of land, if not to an individual farm basis. As I have said, the trend is in that direction.
I am pleased to note that trend and I hope the government will bring in amendments to the act to put it on an individual basis.
When the Prairie Farm Assistance Act is talked about in this house one hears a lot about crop insurance. I have read in the press from time to time where people say that we now have a crop insurance scheme.


I agree with the statement made by the hon. member for Rosthern that as far as the wheat economy on the prairies is concerned, anyone who has made a serious study of a crop insurance scheme on an actuarial basis applied to such an area has recommended against it.

speechtext: What about tobacco?

speechtext:
My hon. friend should be an authority on tobacco, and I would be very glad to hear him speak on that subject. It is probably quite true that a crop insurance scheme, as crop insurance is known to everyone, would not be applicable to a tobacco area, but that is not what I was advocating. I was advocating that the same principle of a government scheme to protect the tobacco growers and make payments to them in years of crop failure be instituted by the government for the very reason that crop insurance is probably impractical in a tobacco area as I know it to be in a wheat growing area.
As my authority, and as one authority that probably the hon. member for Rosthern would accept, I quote from "A Study of Crop Insurance" by the late R. E. Motherwell, B.S.A., printed on August 2, 1944. I want to say that over the years I considered that Dick Motherwell was an outstanding authority in the field of crop insurance. His contribution throughout his too short life to agriculture, in which he believed fundamentally, was outstanding. I am sure that had he been spared he would have made his mark in public life in Canada and would have made an outstanding contribution to the welfare of agriculture, which was his first interest. In the summary on page 66 Mr. Motherwell states:
1.	Completely self-carrying crop insurance has not been successfully achieved for small grains in any country.
2.	Of all ventures in the field of crop insurance the American experiment is the most noteworthy. This experiment showed several things.
(a) That farmers in high-risk areas were unable to pay the premiums necessary for their own protection.
Crop insurance in the strict sense of insurance, according to Mr. Motherwell, if it is to be successful must obtain from each farm unit over a long period of years sufficient premiums to make the crop insurance payments on that particular piece of land in that period of time.
However, there is definite room for improvement in the act. I believe the act should be overhauled along the lines suggested by Mr. Motherwell. One suggestion was that an area such as Manitoba, where the premiums paid in have exceeded the payments out, should receive some special consideration and a zone might be established with different premiums being paid in that area and perhaps even different payments made.

As I have said, there is room for improvement. Certainly the first improvement that must be made should be along the lines suggested by the hon. member for The Battle-fords.
The hon. member for The Battlefords is perfectly justified, in spite of anything said by the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Low), in asking that the payment be doubled without the premium being increased. In 1939 when this act was passed the wheat board had established an initial price for wheat of 70 cents per bushel, with the initial price to the farmer of some 50 cents per bushel. Since that time the price of wheat has gone up two and a half or three times, so as a result the payments into the fund have increased more than the increase suggested by the hon. member for The Battlefords. Therefore it was not necessary for him to ask that the premiums be increased, because with the increased price of wheat the amount of money paid in per bushel has been increased.
I do not want to take any credit away from the government for having passed the act in 1939, but I am critical of the action or inaction of the government since 1939 in permitting the benefits under this act to wither away because of inflation. The benefits obtained today under this act have just a fraction of the purchasing power of the benefits back in 1939. The official 11-factor cost of production index prepared by the bureau of statistics includes the important item of farm implements, building materials, gasoline, oil, grease, feed, fertilizer, binder twine, seed, hardware, tax rates, interest rates and farm wage rates.
This production index prepared by the bureau of statistics, basis 1935-39 equals 100, was 99-3 in 1939 when the act was passed. One year later that index had risen to 106-8. That meant that from the maximum $500 benefit $35 had been taken away in purchasing power through that increase. The Liberal government that put the act on the statute books in one year had taken away $35 of the benefit.
In 1941 the index went up to 116-1 and an additional $37 was taken from the value of the maximum payment. The maximum payment in constant 1939 dollars became $428. In 1942 the index increased to 131-6 and an additional $51 was lost. The $500 payment had become $377. In 1943 the index rose to 143-4 and the value in purchasing power was reduced by $31, making the $500 payment worth $346. In 1944 there was another increase in the index, a loss of another $11 and the value of the payment was down to $335. In 1945 there was another increase in the farmer's cost of production index and an-50433-87
Prairie Farm Assistance Act other $9 was chiselled off the value of prairie farm assistance, bringing the total purchasing power of the $500 payment down to $326.
Mr. Speaker, the figures I am placing on record tonight indicate what this government has done to many measures which it has placed on the statute books and which have been to the benefit of the people to whom they apply. An act is placed on the statute books that provides certain benefits to the people. Then the government, through inflation, allows the benefit to wither away. By allowing inflation to persist year by year, the government has been robbing the western farmer of the purchasing power of prairie farm assistance.
In 1945 the $500 was down to $326; in 1946 it was down to $316; in 1947, it was down to $291; in 1948, it was down to $252; in 1949, it was down to $243; in 1950 it was down to $236; in 1951, it was down to $216 and in 1952 the value of the $500 cheque in 1939 dollars had become just $204. In 1953 the value went up $3, back to $207; and in 1954 the value had increased from $207 to $208. At the rate of increase in the value of prairie farm assistance for that one-year period, if the same rate continues I suppose the Minister of Agriculture might tell the farmers not to worry, that in 300 years the value of prairie farm assistance will be back to its 1939 position.
There is what has happened. The government placed a good act on the statute books in 1939. Since then the farmer has paid and is now paying premiums two and a half to three times as high as those he paid in 1939, and the value of the payment is down to only 42 per cent of the value in 1939. It is no wonder that one municipal council after another and farmer after farmer have been writing to the hon. member for The Battlefords and other members of this house urging them to support the doubling of prairie farm assistance payments.
I should like to see this resolution voted on and passed. I should like to see the payments doubled. I think a strong argument could be made for an even greater increase, but certainly that is the minimum that should be done. There are other improvements that should be made. As I have said, payments should be increased and should be made on a section basis. In keeping with the changing value of the dollar I think the minimum payment under the act should be increased from $200 to $400 and the maximum from $500 to $1,000.
Mr. Speaker, no one in this group wants to detract from any credit coming to the government for having passed and administered the Prairie Farm Assistance Act; but
1366	HOUSE OF
Prairie Farm Assistance Act I appeal to the Minister of Agriculture not to allow these benefits to continue to wither away until this act is unable to provide the protection that all hoped it would provide in 1939. If there is another crop failure in western Canada in 1955 prairie farmers will be back in a position not much better than they were in during the 1930's when this act was placed on the statute books. In western Canada today there are many farmers who have not sufficient money to carry on farming operations for the current year. That would not be so if the prairie farm assistance dollar had kept its 1939 purchasing power. In order to do that the payment should be at least $1,100; for that the government itself, by allowing the dollar value of prairie farm assistance to be reduced, has taken away $600 in purchasing power at today's prices from every farmer in western Canada entitled in 1955 to a full payment under this act.
For the sake of protecting agriculture and the western economy I ask that the government consider this resolution and bring in at this session of parliament an amendment to the act so that payments may be doubled.

Mr. Speaker, in the first place I want to thank the hon. member for Assini-boia (Mr. Argue) for the extremely kind references made to his old fellow student and my late secretary, Mr. Motherwell. He was an expert on this particular question. I also understand that the hon. member for Assini-boia, at the end of his university career, wrote his thesis on this question. He is no doubt as well informed on the question as is any member of the house.
I also want to express my own appreciation to all hon. members who have referred to this legislation in such glowing terms on this occasion. It is rather interesting to look back over 15 years and remember the reception given the legislation when it was brought into the house. There was a great deal of questioning in the minds of members who were here then as to whether or not it would ever work to the satisfaction of the farmers in western Canada and to the benefit of agriculture and the economy of this country in general throughout the years. It is therefore interesting to come back 15 years later and hear members who have made a close study of the question, together with members who have come into the house recently and have found the legislation on the statute books, refer to it as something which is very helpful. I want to say that before I go on to criticize some of the things which have been said.


The act was put on the statute books at the end of a period of about 50 years during which farm organizations all over this continent had been asking for crop insurance of some kind. It had been found almost impossible to find a form of crop insurance which would suit the different crops we have on this continent.
Eventually we worked out a plan which is not insurance. That is one of the reasons we have it. If the amendment to the resolution had not been declared out of order it would have been necessary for me to say that to put it on the basis suggested in the last part of the proposed amendment would have been to make insurance out of it. If we attempted to make insurance out of this act it would have to go to the provincial legislatures, and not be passed in this house. We cannot pass crop insurance in this house unless we amend our constitution. That was decided years ago when we attempted to pass hail insurance in this house. Each of the three prairie provinces moved to have a hail insurance bill passed in the federal house and it was declared at that time that this house did not have the right to pass it.
We therefore passed separate acts out in the three western provinces, and some of that legislation is still in effect. In the province of Saskatchewan we still have hail insurance provided for under the municipal hail insurance act. That is one of the reasons it was never considered, from the beginning, that this was an act to take care of hail insurance. Hail insurance is taken care of under provincial legislation in Saskatchewan. It was taken care of at one time in Alberta and Manitoba as well. I am not sure that those two pieces of legislation are still on the statute books, but certainly the Saskatchewan legislation is still there.

In order to indicate what I mean by that I should like to refer to the statistics with regard to payments.
