Yes, it was rain; everybody was wet and because everybody was wet the crop rusted. There is a very great difference between a rusted crop and a crop failure as the result of drought. Back in 1931 when we had no crop we had to bring our livestock in off the pastures and sell it on the market at about $20 a head. I know, because I brought mine in and sold them. Then we got along with half crops or fairly poor crops until 1937. Then we had another complete crop failure. We had to bring in our livestock and sell them again. We set up pastures all over western Canada and sent out crews who went through the different towns and villages buying up the cattle. The farmers could not get more than a cent and a quarter for this thin stock they were taking from the pastures, but we paid them double that. It was not enough to permit them any earnings whatever.
You cannot compare a condition like that with the condition of 1954. This act was drafted for the purpose of taking care of such conditions. I am one of those who believe that these conditions will return periodically to western Canada. I am not one of those who believe we should take a chance by trying to do anything with this act that would spoil it for the purpose of taking care of drought. It was drafted to take care of drought, and we hope it will be on the statute books in its present form when drought comes back again, as it will.
Within the last few years we had years when the crop was almost as poor as it was back in the thirties. The reason we did not notice it was twofold. In the first place wheat was very high in price and 4, 8 or 10 bushels
Prairie Farm Assistance Act to the acre meant so much more than it did at the time this act was drafted. We went through those conditions, therefore, without very much discussion of the problems that were confronting farmers at that time. As I indicated a few moments ago, we paid out as much as $22 million in one of those years to farmers in areas where there was little or no crop but feed was available within reasonable distance.
What is the condition in the west this year? I know what the condition is on my farm, and we are in the middle of the rust area. Our area was probably not as badly rusted as the area in the constituency of Moose Mountain and particularly in the area between Moose Mountain and the main line of railway. Nevertheless we are in the centre of a strip of country extending from down in Minnesota right up to Lloydminster, which is from 150 to 200 miles wide, that was so badly rusted this year that every rust expert says it was the worst rust epidemic we have ever had in the central part of this continent. Well, I have more feed in my barn this year than I ever had before, and so have a lot of other farmers. We had no feed in our barns back in the years I have been speaking about, because there was none to put in.
This year the rough feed is not so good as it has been in some years. The cattle do not like it as well as they did at other times, because it is rusted. It is not clean straw. Nevertheless we have the feed, and our cattle are not thin. They are not losing weight at all. I had cattle on the Toronto market last week and they brought the top price on that mai'ket. They were fed out in that country. But if I had tried to send them down to Toronto back in 1931, or again in 1937, they never would have reached there. They just could not have stood the trip. But they can go down this year and top the market.
Every farmer out there knows the condition -that is, every farmer who has lived there during times of drought-at the present time is not comparable with that condition at all. And he knows that this act was not brought into being for the particular purpose of dealing with a situation like we have this year at all; but it helps, and they are not grasping at shadows.
That is why they did not pass resolutions about it. They know that to have a resolution passed, of the kind that has been discussed here tonight, to double the rate, would do this legislation more harm than good. Therefore they have hesitated to make any suggestions. I suppose there is a good reason why I should get as many resolutions and letters as anybody else about this thing.

subtopic: RESOLUTION SUGGESTING THAT PAYMENTS UNDER ACT BE DOUBLED
speechtext: Oh, no, they still write. I imagine I have had resolutions from the areas and municipalities from which my hon. friends opposite have had resolutions, and they have indicated to me as a rule to whom they have sent them. There are a few of them, yes, but very few as compared with the days back in the thirties.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: RESOLUTION SUGGESTING THAT PAYMENTS UNDER ACT BE DOUBLED
speechtext: What do you tell them?

subtopic: RESOLUTION SUGGESTING THAT PAYMENTS UNDER ACT BE DOUBLED
speechtext:
The correspondence which comes in now is trivial compared with what it was then. The only resolutions that I have had have come from people who have said, "So and so has called my attention to the fact." Well, now, 1 did not require anybody to call my attention to the facts that existed back in the thirties, when this act was put on the statute books. Everybody had their attention drawn to the facts every time they went out to look at their cattle. They had their attention drawn to the facts every time they looked toward the station to see if the hay being shipped in from Quebec had arrived yet, carrying freight at $18 a ton, and so on.
This is not a condition comparable with that at all. This is a condition under which we had more rain last summer than we knew what to do with. So while up to August our crops looked the best of any we ever saw standing, when the August rust came that grain on the top of the stocks began to disappear or shrivel up, with the result that we have not so much grain. But there is no one in this house who will say we do not have feed, and that we have to go somewhere else for it. The complaint is that we have too much feed grain, and not enough of Nos. 1,
2 and 3 wheat.
Somebody said something about No. 6. Well, one of the characteristics of No. 6 is that you cannot make much flour out of it. But you can feed pigs with it, and you can feed cattle with it. There is nobody complaining about lack of feed. We do not have to ship hay in from away up at Le Pas or Quebec or Minnesota, and certainly in the years immediately before 1939 we were shipping feed in from all those places, giving relief to the farmers everywhere.
This act was put on the statute books because of that experience; but to take it back into the committee on agriculture at present and bring it back into this house in order to amend it would bring up a discussion of conditions so different from those which existed at the time the act was placed on the statute books that most people would begin to wonder why this happened at all.


The farmers know why. The farmers knew that when they did not pass these resolutions which were spoken about, and they still understand it. It is all very well for my hon. friends to laugh, but they do not go to Liberal meetings, you know. When we have Liberal meetings out in Saskatchewan we explain these things. Some of our friends may peek around the corners and look in the doors from outside, but they do not get the full argument. So they come down here to Ottawa and talk as though they are speaking for the farmers when, in fact, the farmers out west know exactly what the situation is. They understand it very well.
Perhaps I should say something about the act itself. The hon. member for Moose Mountain was going to ask me a question this morning. I phoned to tell him I did not have the full information, but that I would get it. He has brought the question up tonight. I have the information before me now.
The question he asked me the other day was whether or not Selkirk wheat was being figured in the computation as to whether certain townships would be paid or would not be paid; that is, whether their crop was less than 8 bushels to the acre or whether it was more than that.
I told him a few days ago when he asked me the question in the house that it was my understanding that the 6 bushel lots which had been turned over by the government to a good many farmers in western Canada to be sown in order to have their Selkirk seed for next year-which is resistant to 15-B rust-did not come into the computation at all. I must say that I have phoned Regina since, and that I did not have exactly the right idea in my own mind at the time. But the facts are true, nevertheless. I thought we had found it necessary in the beginning to say that particular wheat was not taken into the computation. Now I am told that what actually did happen was this: that they checked the municipalities and the Selkirk wheat grown from these 6 bushel lots did not make any difference in any of the municipalities that were checked. Those that were under 8 were sufficiently under that the bringing in of the rule would not have made any difference; and those that were under 4 were sufficiently under that bringing them in did not put them into a higher bracket.
There was only one case left, and presumably it was the one brought up by the hon. member for Moose Mountain tonight. There was one case of one area of which they were not certain until yesterday, and the recheck of that municipality has now been passed, so payments will be made there. So there are no municipalities anywhere in the

three provinces where the 6 bushel amount, or the Selkirk grown on plots seeded by 6 bushel amounts, would make any difference.

subtopic: RESOLUTION SUGGESTING THAT PAYMENTS UNDER ACT BE DOUBLED
speechtext:
My
question was in respect to those contiguous sections which were taken out. I am concerned about individual farmers being taken out under that clause.

subtopic: RESOLUTION SUGGESTING THAT PAYMENTS UNDER ACT BE DOUBLED
speechtext:
They tell me today it will not make any difference to any sized section of country that is under the act. They have gone into that very carefully. If it were going to make any difference we would make a regulation about it, but they say there is no necessity for doing that because it does not affect any of the districts at all.
Well then, we did find it necessary to deal with one feature of it, and we dealt with it some weeks ago by passing an amendment to the regulations. Under the section to which my hon. friend referred-that is, section 5 (g), where we have authority to take out any section of land anywhere in the whole area-the amendment reads like this:
Those portions of land cultivated by any one fanner which were sown to rust-resistant wheat in the year 1954 if the total area so sown comprised 10 or more acres and the average yield thereon was more than 10 bushels per acre.
That comes out, and it neither figures in the computation as to whether the district comes in nor does the individual get any pay as a result of the passing of that regulation if the area remains in. I think that meets with the approval of those who have been bringing the question up. I think it meets with the approval of the hon. member for Moose Mountain who has brought it up more often than anyone else.

subtopic: RESOLUTION SUGGESTING THAT PAYMENTS UNDER ACT BE DOUBLED
speechtext:
I
should like to say to the minister that a farmer could well have 10 acres of Selkirk wheat and have only a part of his farm operation in Selkirk wheat. In other words, he may have 300 additional acres, and surely the minister would not say that should disqualify him because those 300 additional acres may produce a complete crop failure.

subtopic: RESOLUTION SUGGESTING THAT PAYMENTS UNDER ACT BE DOUBLED
speechtext:
Ten acres of Selkirk wheat in Saskatchewan this year means 400 bushels. I have not heard of a crop that was less than 40 bushels to the acre, and that wheat has been selling at as high as $10 a bushel. I am told that in some instances they have been offered $50 for it. The price that has been set by the department is from $5 to $7 a bushel. If they can get $7 a bushel for 400 bushels of wheat it means $2,800 and there is no necessity for any payment under this particular legislation in instances of
Prairie Farm Assistance Act that kind. Therefore we think that the matter is dealt with. The only reason we have set 10 bushels instead of 8 bushels to the acre is that it would be a little difficult to distinguish as between 10 bushels and 8 bushels. In any case there are very few instances of that kind-I do not know of any-where Selkirk wheat got down to 10 bushels to the acre. I do not think anybody is shut out who is being hurt by this method of dealing with it.
I say these things in order to repeat this. We have not forgotten about the changes in conditions. We did not forget about them at the time this act was put through. I have said before, and I am going to repeat now, it took me three months to get this bill through council 15 years ago. Do not run away with the idea that they did not think of pretty nearly everything in bringing up difficulties and suggesting them, and we had to find a way around them. Finally we found it. Then I brought it to this house, and I must say that by the time it got here most hon. members seemed to be in the condition of mind or spirit where they were quite prepared to put it through in a short time, so we got it through in a fairly short time.
It has run along up to now, and I am very pleased that hon. members have found it acceptable, though they think that there might be some little changes made in it. But let me call your attention to this. Bring that act into this house at the present time under the conditions I have described in western Canada and ask this house to double the payments, to pay $50 million instead of paying $25 million-

subtopic: RESOLUTION SUGGESTING THAT PAYMENTS UNDER ACT BE DOUBLED
speechtext:
And it would go through
unanimously.

speechtext: Oh, yes; I have seen-

subtopic: RESOLUTION SUGGESTING THAT PAYMENTS UNDER ACT BE DOUBLED
speechtext: Hon. members would recommend it.

subtopic: RESOLUTION SUGGESTING THAT PAYMENTS UNDER ACT BE DOUBLED
speechtext:
I have seen things go through before, and not many of them go through unanimously. I am quite sure this one would not. I have never brought anything to this house yet in the 20 years I have been here that I could not stand up and defend from A to Z. I certainly could not defend that proposal. If my hon. friends had been a little more considerate of what might be the proper thing to do and just said to increase the payments, there might have been some argument for increasing them a little, though not nearly so much as hon. members have indicated, if you base those increases on the figures I have given.

Prairie Farm Assistance Act
The farmer realizes that he has had better treatment than would be indicated by the figures which were given by hon. members criticizing the act. I am quite sure if this legislation is looked at again, if hon. members will consider it from every point of view, it will go a long way toward settling the troubles that are looked upon as possibilities in the future. I do not think they will be there.

subtopic: RESOLUTION SUGGESTING THAT PAYMENTS UNDER ACT BE DOUBLED
speechtext: Before the minister sits down, will he put on record a statement of the collections from the 1 per cent payment over the areas for which he quoted payments?

subtopic: RESOLUTION SUGGESTING THAT PAYMENTS UNDER ACT BE DOUBLED
speechtext: Well, I will give the totals all together. I will not try to go through them all. From 1939-40 to 1953-54 the collections in Manitoba amounted to $12,465,000. I will just give round figures. In Saskatchewan the collections amounted to $44,343,000; in Alberta, $22,885,000; and unallocated, $14,744. Some of those I presume would be from the area in British Columbia. The total is $79,708,145. In Manitoba, the expenditures amounted to $3,924,000; in Saskatchewan, $104,969,000; in Alberta, $36,921,000; other payments, British Columbia largely, $290,526. The total is $146,105,000. If you want to get the total down to the end of March this year you will have to add approximately $25 million.

speechtext: That is the payments.

subtopic: RESOLUTION SUGGESTING THAT PAYMENTS UNDER ACT BE DOUBLED

subtopic: RESOLUTION SUGGESTING THAT PAYMENTS UNDER ACT BE DOUBLED
speechtext: When the minister is putting these tables on record will he also give us the districts that are paying into this fund and getting nothing out of it?

subtopic: RESOLUTION SUGGESTING THAT PAYMENTS UNDER ACT BE DOUBLED
speechtext:
The hon. member for Selkirk has been coming back to that. I am sorry he was not here during the last two or three years when we dealt with some of these things. But he is back again, and I have no hesitation in explaining the matter to him.
When this legislation was put on the statute books it was to cover the wheat growing areas, and when we put it on we explained that one of the reasons it was necessary to have it was that the administration of the natural resources, including the lands of the prairies, was carried on from Ottawa for a considerable time. They put

people in areas where it was too dry to farm, and some of them had to be moved off.
When the hon. member for Assiniboia gave the figures a few moments ago of the number of farmers we had in that area some years ago and the number we have now, he forgot to state that we moved a lot of people off those lands. We moved them off because the land was too dry for them to farm. We put the lands into pastures to help the farmers who were living around about the pastures. Some were moved over into the neighbourhood of the rolling hills at Brooks. Some of them we are moving now into the area around Vauxhall in Alberta. Many of them were moved to other sections of the province of Saskatchewan, but still outside that area.
We moved those people; but the question my hon. friend asks me is, what about the area up between the lakes? They are not able to benefit under this act. We amended the act, I think in 1947 or somewhere around there, because we found that some people were being put back on those lands in certain areas by the provincial authorities. Some people were being put back on the lands that we had taken them off, and so we brought in legislation providing that if the provincial government put anyone on those lands, or on any other lands, from 1940 down to a certain date, it was presumed that they had put them in under conditions where they could make a living without having the benefits of this act. We said that if the act was to be made to apply to everybody, if anyone bought that land afterward then this government would be asked to pay something we do not think we should pay. Therefore we took the matter to the agriculture committee and thrashed it out there. Then we decided where the line should be run in Alberta. We were not able to decide where it should run in Saskatchewan and Manitoba until a year later. A year later we decided the lines there, saying that this particular amendment would not apply to anyone who came in north of those lines.
That is the reason some of those people over in that area are not able to draw benefits. But I call the attention of my hon. friend to the fact that everybody in Montreal who is a taxpayer pays into this; everybody in Toronto who is a taxpayer pays; everybody in Vancouver who is a taxpayer pays, and so with Regina, Saskatoon and everywhere else.

subtopic: RESOLUTION SUGGESTING THAT PAYMENTS UNDER ACT BE DOUBLED
speechtext: I was coming around to telling you; I expected my hon. friend would say something like that. My hon. friend says they are paying in the 1 per cent in these areas and they are not being paid. But the 1 per cent which is paid does not equal the amount being paid out of revenues. My hon. friend spoke about his area. What about Gladstone right across the lake? There is not a chance of the people in Gladstone municipality drawing under this act as a rule, as they have not had a crop failure, unless it is this year because of rust. Take the municipality in which I live. We have not come under this act at any time, yet we pay in our 1 per cent. That is the principle underlying any co-operative effort; it goes right back to biblical days. We bear one another's burdens. We are told that people who want to help out should give of their substance, and so we are saying that everybody should help. My hon. friend called something to my attention a moment ago.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Tomorrow we shall consider the motion that Mr. Speaker do leave the chair for the house to resolve itself into committee of supply. When that is completed we shall take up the resolution standing in the name of the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Lapointe) with respect to the War Veterans Allowance Act. We shall then take up Bill No. 3.
I should like to draw the attention of hon. members to the fact that there are six or seven comparatively innocuous resolutions on the order paper that I think we should dispose of fairly soon in order to get some work done and ready for the other place. I would ask hon. members to take a look at them to see if we could not arrange to dispose of them in short order some day that can be agreed on. These are items Nos. 13, 14, 21, 24, 27, 31 and 32.
Business of the House

I suppose that once we get into supply the estimates of three departments will be referred to the estimates committee. Can the minister tell us this evening which estimates will be considered first in the committee? It is essential to have that information because it may be necessary to make certain changes in the personnel of the estimates committee.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I am not a member of the committee, so I would not want to say what they would decide to do. But if the committee chose to consider the estimates of citizenship and immigration first that would be agreeable to us.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Can the minister tell us how many departments will be called if we do get into supply some time tomorrow?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: We would like to call six in order to provide as follows: three to go to the committee on estimates; one, external affairs, to be made available for further discussion if it is found desirable to do that and two to be made available to the committee of supply itself for consideration. It may be that hon. members will feel that there ought to be only one for that purpose, but I think they will agree that with supply on Thursdays and Fridays it would be convenient to have two departments for the government to call, depending on what minister may be available.

The minister has a very kindly way of making these suggestions. However, we do feel that putting in six departments at once is asking for one too many. We suggest that five be set by the government on this occasion. Is that satisfactory?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Let us settle for four.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I have no objection to limiting the number to five. I do point out, however, that we have agreed to send four or five to the estimates committee, and we are being asked to keep that down to three. I had hoped that the estimates committee would have some estimates to deal with at the earliest possible moment so they will not be considering estimates in May or June, when we ought to be dealing with them in the house.
They are going to deal with the estimates of just one department at a time?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Citizenship will be there for some time.

It being ten minutes after ten o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
